title: Why It's So Hard to Be a Nurse
srt:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:12,974
Three forty in the morning. Room four has stopped breathing, and you're standing in the corridor holding a coffee that isn't even yours. You put it down. Gently. It's the calmest thing you'll do tonight.

2
00:00:13,374 --> 00:00:26,740
You've been awake for twenty hours. This is your third night in a row, and your body has stopped asking questions. To understand how you got here, rewind to seven p.m. You were smiling then.

3
00:00:27,140 --> 00:00:40,963
Handover. The day nurse hands you five patients, a list longer than your arm, and a printer that chews the medication sheet. Every night. You've named the printer. You don't say the name out loud.

4
00:00:41,363 --> 00:00:53,532
On paper, the shift is twelve hours. In practice, there's charting, there's the family who read something online, and there's the patient who needs you at seven oh one. Nobody counts that hour. You do.

5
00:00:53,932 --> 00:01:05,970
You're entitled to a thirty-minute break. Seven out of ten nurses regularly skip it. Tonight you're one of them: a granola bar, standing up, in a supply closet, between two boxes of gloves.

6
00:01:06,370 --> 00:01:17,799
The bathroom is thirty seconds away. You pass it going to room two. You pass it coming back. You'll pass it fourteen times before you go in. Your bladder has filed a formal complaint.

7
00:01:18,199 --> 00:01:32,566
Midnight. Room two rings every ten minutes: water, pillow, the TV remote, water again. Room four never rings. Not once. And somewhere in your tired brain, that's the one that bothers you.

8
00:01:32,966 --> 00:01:46,854
Three a.m. is when the human body most wants to sleep. By some cosmic joke, it's also when everyone on the floor needs you at once. Nobody designed this. It just happens. To you. Every night.

9
00:01:47,254 --> 00:01:59,358
Three forty. Room four. You put down the coffee and you run, and for the next ninety seconds nothing else in the world exists. That part of the story is next. You already know you'll be there.

title: Why It's So Hard to Be a Delivery Courier
alts: - Why It Sucks to Be a Delivery Courier
desc:
It's 9:47 p.m., it's raining sideways, and you're on the fourteenth floor of a building with no elevator. Inside the bag is soup.

This is one shift as a food delivery courier, lived from the inside: a green button instead of a boss, a bag the size of a fridge, a lunch rush that turns the map red, a parking lot full of people waiting for their phones to buzz, and the one customer who says "just leave it."

Based on real research:
• Most New York couriers surveyed said restaurants never let them use the bathroom — Los Deliveristas Unidos / Cornell ILR, 2021
• Nearly half of deactivated gig workers were later found to have done nothing wrong — Human Rights Watch, "The Gig Trap", 2025
• Time spent waiting for orders counts as unpaid time — NYC DCWP data, 2025

srt:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:13,823
Nine forty-seven p.m. It's raining sideways. You are on the fourteenth floor of a building whose elevator has been "under maintenance" since spring, holding a bag that is dripping. Inside the bag is soup.

2
00:00:14,223 --> 00:00:28,329
You knock. Nothing. You knock again. A voice from behind the door says: "Just leave it." You look at the soup. The soup looks at you. Neither of you is going to talk about the stairs.

3
00:00:28,729 --> 00:00:38,024
You've been on the bike for eleven hours. To understand how you ended up here, with soup, go back to this morning, when the app said it was going to be a great day.

4
00:00:38,424 --> 00:00:50,397
Seven thirty. You press "Go online." That's the whole onboarding. No manager, no desk, no colleagues. Just a green button and a bag the size of a small fridge strapped to your back.

5
00:00:50,797 --> 00:01:03,358
The first order comes in nine seconds later. Two coffees. Four kilometers. The app shows you the money, and the money is fine. The money is always fine until you divide it by the minutes.

6
00:01:03,758 --> 00:01:16,863
You arrive at the café. The coffees are not ready. You stand in the corner by the napkins, the way couriers stand: not in the way, but not quite welcome either. The clock is running. Your pay is not.

7
00:01:17,263 --> 00:01:31,630
Eleven minutes later, the coffees are ready. You ride. You deliver. The customer says "thanks" without looking up. The app asks you to rate the experience. You give it five stars. You always give five stars.

8
00:01:32,030 --> 00:01:40,803
By ten a.m., you've done six orders and your legs have found their rhythm. This is the good part of the day. Remember it. You'll need it around four.

9
00:01:41,203 --> 00:01:51,978
Twelve o'clock. The map turns red. Every restaurant in the city has decided to cook at the same time, and every person in the city has decided they can't walk two hundred meters.

10
00:01:52,378 --> 00:02:04,612
The app starts stacking: pick up here, then here, deliver there, then there. Four bags, two hands, one bike. You become a very fast game of Tetris with a heartbeat.

11
00:02:05,012 --> 00:02:19,184
Order two is on the fifth floor. "Leave at the door," the note says. You leave it at the door. You're back on the bike when the phone rings. "Where's my order?" At the door. "Which door?" Yours.

12
00:02:19,584 --> 00:02:31,883
Order three is a family-size pizza. Pizza is the enemy. Pizza is flat, wide, and takes the full bag. Every bump in the road is a decision about where the cheese ends up.

13
00:02:32,283 --> 00:02:42,449
Order four tipped in the app. Order four's tip is listed as "pending." It will stay pending. You've stopped checking. The app knows this about you, and it's fine with it.

14
00:02:42,849 --> 00:02:53,080
One thirty. The red fades. You've done fourteen orders in ninety minutes, and the city goes back to pretending it doesn't need you. Until dinner.

15
00:02:53,480 --> 00:03:04,974
Three p.m. is nothing. No orders. You sit on your bike in a parking lot with eleven other people on their bikes in the same parking lot, all looking at the same screen, all waiting.

16
00:03:05,374 --> 00:03:17,412
Your phone is at thirty-one percent. Your phone is your job. If it dies, you don't exist. You have a power bank, a second power bank, and a cable held together with tape.

17
00:03:17,812 --> 00:03:31,635
Now, the question nobody asks: where do you go to the bathroom? In one survey of New York couriers, most said restaurants simply never let them in. So the answer is: a gas station. Far away.

18
00:03:32,035 --> 00:03:45,859
You do the math on a napkin. Hours online: seven and a half. Money earned: not bad. Money per hour of being actually paid: a different number. You fold the napkin and put it away.

19
00:03:46,259 --> 00:03:56,490
Four p.m. The sky changes its mind. You feel the first drop on your helmet, and somewhere in the city, ten thousand people decide that tonight, they're not cooking.

20
00:03:56,890 --> 00:04:13,586
Rain means orders. Rain means money. Rain also means wet gloves, fogged glasses, and brakes that work on a slight delay. The app adds a small bonus. The road adds a small risk. Nobody tells you which is bigger.

21
00:04:13,986 --> 00:04:28,288
The bag is waterproof, mostly. Your jacket is waterproof, mostly. You are waterproof, not at all. By six, there is a river running down your spine into places a river shouldn't go.

22
00:04:28,688 --> 00:04:43,927
Seven p.m. A customer messages: "Can you hurry?" You are on a bike, in the rain, at a red light. You type "On my way." You've typed "On my way" so many times your phone suggests it before you start.

23
00:04:44,327 --> 00:04:55,951
Eight p.m. The building with no elevator again. Different customer, same stairs. Fourteen floors. You've started counting them. Not the steps. The floors. The steps would be depressing.

24
00:04:56,351 --> 00:05:09,042
Your rating today is four point nine. Yesterday it was five. Somebody gave you one star. You'll never know who, or why, and the app won't tell you. It just remembers.

25
00:05:09,442 --> 00:05:22,873
Nine forty-seven. Fourteenth floor. The soup. "Just leave it." You leave it. You take the stairs down, because the stairs are the only thing in this job that's always exactly where it said it would be.

26
00:05:23,273 --> 00:05:36,313
Here's what the day looks like from above: twelve hours online, roughly forty kilometers of city, around forty orders, and one actual meal, eaten standing next to a dumpster that smelled better than it looked.

27
00:05:36,713 --> 00:05:51,341
No sick days. No bad-weather days. If the app decides you're done, you're done. One report found that nearly half of the couriers it deactivated were later found to have done nothing wrong. The app does not apologize. It doesn't have the feature.

28
00:05:51,741 --> 00:06:07,698
Eleven forty p.m. You press "Go offline." The app asks you to rate your day. You give it five stars. You always give five stars. Then you ride home, in the dark, with an empty bag that finally weighs nothing.

29
00:06:08,098 --> 00:06:19,200
Tomorrow, you'll press the green button again. Not because the app is kind, but because the city will still want its soup, and you are the only one who knows about the stairs.

30
00:06:19,600 --> 00:06:28,765
That was one shift. Next time: a different job, a different door. Subscribe if you want to be there. The soup, probably, will still be waiting.

title: Why It's So Hard to Be a Teacher
desc:
It's 10:52 p.m. Notebook 117 of 150. The red pen is dying, and the essay is one sentence long.

This is one day as a teacher, lived from the inside: a copier with moods, twenty-eight kids and one asleep, fractions explained four ways, a twenty-minute lunch eaten next to the copier, a meeting about the next meeting, and a tote bag of notebooks that wears a seatbelt.

Based on real research:
• Full-time teachers work about 41 hours a week; only about 23 of them are teaching — OECD TALIS 2024
• Teachers spend close to $900 a year of their own money on the classroom — AdoptAClassroom Teacher Spending Survey, 2025
• 44% of new teachers leave within five years by one widely cited estimate; a federal cohort study found 17% — Ingersoll (UPenn); NCES 2015

srt:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:13,627
Ten fifty-two p.m. Your kitchen table. Notebook one hundred and seventeen out of one hundred and fifty. The red pen is dying. The essay is called "My Summer," and the kid wrote one sentence.

2
00:00:14,027 --> 00:00:22,931
You read the sentence twice. You put the pen down. Somewhere in the house a dishwasher finishes, and that is the most exciting thing that will happen to you tonight.

3
00:00:23,331 --> 00:00:33,170
You've been awake since five forty. To understand how you ended up here, with notebook one seventeen, rewind to this morning, when you still believed in the lesson plan.

4
00:00:33,570 --> 00:00:47,676
Six forty. The school is empty and the copier is already jammed. The copier has moods. Today's mood is "paper tray two." You fix it with a ruler and a word you'll never say in class.

5
00:00:48,076 --> 00:01:01,377
Seven thirty. First bell. Twenty-eight kids. Three absent, one asleep, one who did the homework for a different subject, and one who is quietly the smartest person in the building and does not know it yet.

6
00:01:01,777 --> 00:01:11,812
You take attendance. You collect phones. You collect the phones again, because the first collection was a decoy. You smile. The smile is part of the uniform.

7
00:01:12,212 --> 00:01:27,842
Period one is fractions. You explain fractions. You explain fractions a second way, a third way, with pizza, with money, with a song you regret immediately. On the fourth way, it lands. For four kids.

8
00:01:28,242 --> 00:01:40,737
A hand goes up. "Will this be on the test?" You say yes. It will not be on the test. But now, for the next forty minutes, it is the most important thing in the room. That's the trick.

9
00:01:41,137 --> 00:01:55,178
Period three. Fire drill. Twenty-eight kids, one door, zero sense of urgency. You count heads in the parking lot. Twenty-seven. Then twenty-eight. The last one went back for his snack.

10
00:01:55,578 --> 00:02:07,812
Period four. A kid asks a question you don't know the answer to. You say "great question, let's find out together." This is teacher for "I will Google this tonight at eleven."

11
00:02:08,212 --> 00:02:18,835
Lunch is twenty minutes. The line takes thirteen. You eat the remaining seven standing next to the copier, which is jammed again, as a kind of companionship.

12
00:02:19,235 --> 00:02:29,271
You pass the staff bathroom four times before you go in. If this sounds familiar, you've met the nurse from episode one. Same door, different building, same bladder.

13
00:02:29,671 --> 00:02:43,233
Your phone shows an email from a parent. Subject: "Quick question." The email is six hundred words long. The question is in paragraph four. You answer it at eleven p.m., in two sentences.

14
00:02:43,633 --> 00:02:57,260
Period six is the one after lunch, which means twenty-eight kids powered entirely by sugar and grudges. You teach anyway. Nobody films this part. It would not go viral.

15
00:02:57,660 --> 00:03:09,829
You run out of whiteboard markers. The school gave you a budget in September. The budget was gone by October. The markers come from your own wallet, like the stickers, the tissues, and the extra pencils.

16
00:03:10,229 --> 00:03:21,331
On average, a teacher in the US spends close to nine hundred dollars a year of their own money on the classroom. Nobody signs a receipt for that. The kids think the markers just appear.

17
00:03:21,731 --> 00:03:33,899
You keep a drawer of granola bars. Not for you. For the kid who didn't eat breakfast, who will not say so, and who gets very quiet around ten a.m. You've learned to read quiet.

18
00:03:34,299 --> 00:03:45,075
Three fifteen. The bell. The kids leave in eleven seconds. You do not leave. There's bus duty, which is standing in the wind pointing at buses.

19
00:03:45,475 --> 00:03:55,510
Four p.m. A meeting about the next meeting. There are slides. There is a word on the slides that was invented last year and will be retired next year. You nod at the word.

20
00:03:55,910 --> 00:04:07,818
Five thirty. You finally sit at your desk. It is the first time you've sat today. Your knees file a complaint. You open your laptop, and the real job begins: the one nobody sees.

21
00:04:08,218 --> 00:04:23,173
Here's the math from the OECD: a full-time teacher works about forty-one hours a week. Only about twenty-three of those are actual teaching. The rest is planning, grading, emails, and meetings about meetings.

22
00:04:23,573 --> 00:04:34,479
Seven p.m. You drive home with a tote bag of notebooks on the passenger seat. It has a seatbelt on. You're not sure when that started. You're not sure it's a joke anymore.

23
00:04:34,879 --> 00:04:50,988
Dinner is standing up. Then the table, the pen, the stack. One hundred and fifty notebooks, two minutes each, is five hours. You have three. You do the math on a sticky note and stop doing the math.

24
00:04:51,388 --> 00:05:04,688
Somewhere around notebook sixty, the handwriting starts to blur together, and you catch yourself writing "good job" on a page that says nothing. You cross it out. You write a real comment. It takes longer.

25
00:05:05,088 --> 00:05:15,712
Your rating today was a kid saying "this was actually okay" on the way out. You will remember it for a week. You will remember the other comment, the one from Tuesday, for a year.

26
00:05:16,112 --> 00:05:33,200
One widely cited estimate says forty-four percent of new teachers leave within five years. A federal study that followed one group found closer to seventeen. The honest answer is: a lot, and it depends who's counting.

27
00:05:33,600 --> 00:05:45,507
The ones who stay don't stay for the money, the hours, or the copier. They stay for the kid in the back row, the one who doesn't know yet. You've already picked yours this year.

28
00:05:45,907 --> 00:06:01,668
Eleven thirty. Notebook one seventeen. "My Summer." One sentence: "My summer was good. I was with my grandma. She is gone now." You pick up the red pen. You put it down. You pick up a sticker.

29
00:06:02,068 --> 00:06:17,567
Eleven forty. Notebook one fifty. You close it. The dishwasher is quiet. Tomorrow the alarm says five forty, and the copier will be waiting, and so will twenty-eight kids, one of them still asleep.

30
00:06:17,967 --> 00:06:26,740
That was one day. Next time: a different job, a different door. Subscribe if you want to be there. Bring your own markers.

title: Why It's So Hard to Be a Line Cook
desc:
It's 9:14 p.m. on a Saturday. Forty-one tickets on the rail, a burn you don't remember getting, and table twelve wants the salmon medium-well.

This is one day as a line cook, lived from the inside: forty pounds of onions, the walk-in as the only quiet place in the building, a ticket printer that sounds like a machine gun by seven, six pans on four burners, an allergy ticket done right in ninety seconds, the 86 board that doesn't help, and eleven minutes with a mop and the music turned up.

Based on real research:
• The median cook in the US earns $17.19 an hour, about $35,760 a year — U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook, May 2024 data
• In full-service restaurants, cuts bad enough to miss work happen at 23.6 cases per 10,000 full-time workers vs 7.1 across private industry; thermal burns at 10.2 vs 1.5 — BLS, Injuries, Illnesses, and Fatalities, 2019
• Monthly separations in accommodation and food services ran about 5–6% through 2023–24 vs about 3% for the whole economy — BLS Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey

srt:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:12,822
Nine fourteen p.m. Saturday. The ticket printer has not stopped in forty minutes. There are forty-one tickets on the rail. Table twelve wants the salmon medium-well, and you did not know salmon had a medium-well.

2
00:00:13,222 --> 00:00:23,997
Your left forearm has a new burn from six forty. You don't remember getting it. The burn is shaped like the edge of a sauté pan, because it is the edge of a sauté pan.

3
00:00:24,397 --> 00:00:36,631
You've been standing since one p.m. To understand how you ended up here, holding a fish and an opinion, rewind to the afternoon, when the kitchen was quiet and you still had a plan.

4
00:00:37,031 --> 00:00:53,140
One p.m. The kitchen is cold, the radio is on, and there are forty pounds of onions. You dice all of them. Your eyes stop crying after bag two. That is not a metaphor. Your eyes just gave up.

5
00:00:53,540 --> 00:01:06,362
Prep is the part nobody sees. Sauces, stocks, portioned proteins, herbs picked leaf by leaf. Every plate tonight was built now, in silence, by a guy in a backwards cap with a very sharp knife.

6
00:01:06,762 --> 00:01:18,190
The walk-in cooler is thirty-eight degrees. It is also the only place in the building where you can stand still for ten seconds. People go in for lemons. People stay for the silence.

7
00:01:18,590 --> 00:01:33,546
Three thirty. Family meal: the staff eats together, standing, out of a hotel pan. It is the best meal you'll have today. It is also the only one. You eat it in four minutes, like a raccoon with a schedule.

8
00:01:33,946 --> 00:01:43,241
Five p.m. Doors. The first ticket prints. It makes a small, polite sound. By seven, it will sound like a machine gun that hates you personally.

9
00:01:43,641 --> 00:02:04,865
The line is six feet wide and about four hundred degrees. Grill, sauté, fryer, the pass. Four people, no room, one rule: say where you are. "Behind." "Hot." "Corner." You will say "behind" two hundred times tonight. Nobody has ever said it back to you at home.

10
00:02:05,265 --> 00:02:20,090
Seven forty. The rush. Tickets come faster than plates leave. You have six pans on four burners, which is a math problem you solve with your hands. Everything is either burning or not ready. There is no third state.

11
00:02:20,490 --> 00:02:31,722
A ticket comes back. Table twelve. The salmon was, and this is a quote, "too fishy." You refire it. You smile at the fish. The fish understands.

12
00:02:32,122 --> 00:02:46,490
There is an allergy ticket. Severe. Nuts. You change gloves, change the board, change the pan, change the tongs. You do it in ninety seconds, and you do it right, because this is the one ticket tonight that isn't about dinner.

13
00:02:46,890 --> 00:02:59,516
"Eighty-six the lamb." Which means the lamb is gone. Eleven tables ordered it anyway. Each server comes back to tell you the news personally. You write it on the board. The board does not help.

14
00:02:59,916 --> 00:03:08,688
You do not go to the bathroom. If this sounds familiar, you've met the nurse, the courier and the teacher. Same bladder, hotter room.

15
00:03:09,088 --> 00:03:25,328
Here is what the hands pay. In full-service restaurants, cuts bad enough to miss work happen about three times as often as across all private industry. Burns, almost seven times as often. That's the Bureau of Labor Statistics, not the chef on TV.

16
00:03:25,728 --> 00:03:38,288
You have a burn from tonight, a cut from Tuesday, and a scar from a different restaurant that you point to like a souvenir. Cooks compare them. Nobody wins. Everyone has a story about a fryer.

17
00:03:38,688 --> 00:03:49,529
Your feet have been on a rubber mat for eight hours. Your knees have an opinion. Your back has a petition. You are thirty-one years old and you walk like a chair.

18
00:03:49,929 --> 00:04:05,429
The median cook in America makes about seventeen dollars and nineteen cents an hour. That's thirty-five thousand seven hundred sixty a year, before the burns. The chef on TV makes that in one episode, and he doesn't do dishes.

19
00:04:05,829 --> 00:04:18,454
Tips go to the front of the house. You are the back of the house. The wall between you is three feet thick and made of a heat lamp. Every night, somebody out there thanks the server for the sauce you made at two p.m.

20
00:04:18,854 --> 00:04:34,484
People leave this industry fast. In food service, about one in eighteen workers leaves their job every month. Across the whole economy, it's about one in thirty-three. Over a year, that is most of the kitchen, gone and replaced.

21
00:04:34,884 --> 00:04:47,706
Ten thirty. Last ticket. Table twelve, again, because of course. Dessert. You plate it like it's the first one tonight, because the person eating it doesn't know it's the last.

22
00:04:48,106 --> 00:04:59,339
Then the clean-down. You scrape the flattop, pull the fryer oil, bleach the boards, wrap forty containers, and label every one with tape and a marker in handwriting only you can read.

23
00:04:59,739 --> 00:05:12,365
Eleven forty. The floor gets mopped. The mop gets mopped. The music is yours now, and it's loud, and for eleven minutes the kitchen is the best place on earth.

24
00:05:12,765 --> 00:05:22,060
The chef says "good push." Two words. You'll run them back in your head on the bus. You will not tell anyone that you did that.

25
00:05:22,460 --> 00:05:33,018
Twelve twenty a.m. The bus. You smell like fryer oil and lemons. The person next to you moves one seat over. You understand. You would also move.

26
00:05:33,418 --> 00:05:47,393
One ten a.m. Home. You eat cereal standing at the counter, because sitting feels like a decision. You watch a cooking show. You yell at it. You go to bed at two.

27
00:05:47,793 --> 00:06:01,551
So why do it. Not the money. Not the hours. Not the burns. It's the eleven minutes with the mop and the music. It's "good push." It's a plate leaving the pass exactly the way you saw it in your head.

28
00:06:01,951 --> 00:06:15,513
And it's the people. The four of you, six feet of steel, four hundred degrees, two hundred "behinds," and not one dropped plate. Nobody films that part either. It would not go viral.

29
00:06:15,913 --> 00:06:26,079
Tomorrow starts at one p.m. There will be onions. There will be a table twelve. There is always a table twelve. You already know what you'll say to the fish.

30
00:06:26,479 --> 00:06:39,453
That was one day. Next time: a different job, a different door. Subscribe if you want to be there. And please, for everyone's sake, don't order the salmon medium-well.

title: Why It's So Hard to Be a Truck Driver
desc:
It's 4:50 a.m. Your bed is a shelf behind two seats, your window is a rest area in Nebraska, and a black box on the dashboard has already started counting.

This is one day as a long-haul truck driver, lived from the inside: eighteen tires checked with a flashlight, a seventy-two-foot vehicle, a 7:30 appointment that becomes a 10:15 dock, two hours of unpaid "detention", a GPS that wants you under a twelve-foot bridge, a thirty-minute break that is the only time the clock stops, and fifty-six minutes a day looking for somewhere to park it all.

Based on real research:
• Median pay for heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers: $57,440 a year, $27.62 an hour — U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook, May 2024
• Hours of service: 11 hours driving, 14-hour window, 30-minute break by hour 8, 60/70 hours in 7/8 days, 34-hour restart — FMCSA, Summary of Hours of Service Regulations
• Detention (waiting beyond two hours at a facility) reported at 39.3% of stops; shippers pay roughly half of detention invoices — American Transportation Research Institute, Costs and Consequences of Truck Driver Detention, 2024
• Drivers spend an average of 56 minutes a day looking for parking, about $4,600 a year in lost wages — ATRI Truck Parking Diary study, 2016
• 823 heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers died on the job in 2023, more than any other single occupation — BLS Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries 2023
• Driver turnover at large truckload carriers averaged roughly 90% a year through the 2010s — American Trucking Associations

srt:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:11,898
Four fifty in the morning. Your alarm is your phone, your bed is a shelf behind two seats, and your window is a rest area in Nebraska. You have eleven hours of driving today. Your clock started the second you touched the steering wheel.

2
00:00:12,298 --> 00:00:22,984
You are not late. You are never late. You are legally forbidden from being late, because the little black box on your dashboard counts every minute you work, and when it says stop, you stop. Wherever you are.

3
00:00:23,384 --> 00:00:31,672
To understand why you sleep in a parking lot by choice, rewind to yesterday morning, when you still had a plan, a full thermos, and no idea where you'd be tonight.

4
00:00:32,072 --> 00:00:45,299
Five a.m. Before you drive one foot, you walk around eighty thousand pounds of truck with a flashlight. Tires, brakes, lights, mirrors, the fifth wheel. Eighteen tires. You kick none of them. You check all of them.

5
00:00:45,699 --> 00:00:55,032
The trailer is fifty-three feet long. Your truck is seventy-two feet from bumper to bumper. You will park this thing tonight in a space designed by someone who has never parked anything.

6
00:00:55,432 --> 00:01:08,019
You log on. The black box is called an electronic logging device, and it knows four things about you: driving, on duty, off duty, sleeper. It does not know "stuck." It does not know "hungry." It only knows time.

7
00:01:08,419 --> 00:01:21,290
The rules fit on a card. Eleven hours of driving. A fourteen-hour window to do it in. A thirty-minute break by hour eight. Seventy hours in eight days, then thirty-four hours off. You know this card better than your own phone number.

8
00:01:21,690 --> 00:01:31,854
Seven thirty. The warehouse. Your appointment is at seven thirty. You check in at seven thirty. A man in a vest says, "Dock twelve, we'll call you." Nobody calls you.

9
00:01:32,254 --> 00:01:41,872
You wait. Your fourteen-hour window does not wait. It started at five. Every minute at this dock is a minute you will not have on the highway tonight, and the black box knows it.

10
00:01:42,272 --> 00:01:54,050
Nine forty. Two hours and ten minutes. Officially, this is now "detention." Drivers report it at about four in ten stops. You are paid by the mile. The last two hours paid exactly zero miles.

11
00:01:54,450 --> 00:02:04,662
Your company will send the shipper a bill for your time. The shipper will pay about half of those bills. You will see none of it either way. You are, technically, furniture in this parking lot.

12
00:02:05,062 --> 00:02:17,268
Ten fifteen. "Dock twelve." You back fifty-three feet of trailer into a slot with two inches on each side, using two mirrors and a feeling. You do it in one try. Nobody claps. You've stopped expecting it.

13
00:02:17,668 --> 00:02:29,257
Ten forty. Finally, the highway. Interstate eighty, westbound. Your speed is sixty-five. Your mind is on tonight. You have about six hours left in the window and five hundred miles of wanting.

14
00:02:29,657 --> 00:02:37,423
You do not go to the bathroom. If this sounds familiar, you've met the nurse, the courier, the teacher and the cook. Same bladder, bigger vehicle.

15
00:02:37,823 --> 00:02:47,939
Lunch is a gas station sandwich eaten at the wheel, because stopping costs you thirty minutes and thirty minutes is forty miles. There is a cooler behind your seat with a plan in it. The plan was salad.

16
00:02:48,339 --> 00:03:01,448
Here is what the body pays. In 2023, eight hundred twenty-three truck drivers died on the job in America. More than any other occupation. Not the most dangerous rate, the most people. You are one of about two million of them.

17
00:03:01,848 --> 00:03:13,199
Your thirty-minute break. The law says by hour eight. You take it at a rest area, in the sleeper, eyes closed, not asleep. The clock is paused. It is the only time all day the clock is paused.

18
00:03:13,599 --> 00:03:24,951
The GPS is lying again. It wants you on a bridge with a twelve-foot clearance. Your trailer is thirteen and a half. You know this because you check, every time, because someone, somewhere, once didn't.

19
00:03:25,351 --> 00:03:34,897
The median truck driver in America makes about fifty-seven thousand four hundred forty dollars a year. That's twenty-seven dollars and sixty-two cents an hour, if you only count the hours they count.

20
00:03:35,297 --> 00:03:47,860
But you are not paid by the hour. You are paid by the mile. So the dock paid nothing, the inspection paid nothing, the break paid nothing, and the hour you'll spend looking for parking tonight will pay nothing. Your truck earns. You wait.

21
00:03:48,260 --> 00:03:57,711
At the big carriers, turnover has run around ninety percent a year for most of a decade. Nine out of ten seats, new person. The trucks don't change. The drivers do.

22
00:03:58,111 --> 00:04:07,112
Five fifteen p.m. The hunt. You have about an hour of legal driving left, and you need a parking space for a seventy-two-foot vehicle in a country that forgot to build them.

23
00:04:07,512 --> 00:04:18,008
Drivers spend on average fifty-six minutes a day looking for parking. Almost an hour of your eleven. That's about forty-six hundred dollars a year of driving time, spent circling lots that are already full.

24
00:04:18,408 --> 00:04:30,804
The first truck stop: full. The second: full, and someone has parked a pickup across two spaces. The third has one spot, at the end, next to a dumpster, nose to the highway. It's yours. It's beautiful.

25
00:04:31,204 --> 00:04:41,535
Six twenty. You stop. Not because you want to. Because the box says so. Your fourteen-hour window closes at seven, and you will be inside it, parked, with eleven minutes to spare.

26
00:04:41,935 --> 00:04:51,814
The shower costs a token you get for buying fuel. You buy eighty gallons of fuel. The shower is the best eight minutes of your day. You rate it. Four stars. The water pressure.

27
00:04:52,214 --> 00:05:02,615
Dinner is a microwave burrito eaten on the shelf you sleep on, watching a phone propped against a pillow. Somebody on it is explaining why truckers are lonely. You hit the like button. You don't finish it.

28
00:05:03,015 --> 00:05:15,079
Ten p.m. You call home. Someone says the dog did a thing. You laugh at the right place. You are two thousand miles from the dog. You will be home Saturday. Probably. The box decides.

29
00:05:15,479 --> 00:05:28,232
So why do it. Because somewhere behind you is a warehouse that was empty and now isn't. Because the highway at five a.m. with the sun coming up over Wyoming is the best view in any office in America. Because you are very, very good at backing up.

30
00:05:28,632 --> 00:05:43,545
That was one day. Tomorrow starts at four fifty, with a flashlight and eighteen tires. Next time: a different job, a different door. Subscribe if you want to be there. And if you see a truck looking for parking tonight, that pickup across two spaces? Move it.

title: Why It's So Hard to Be a Flight Attendant
desc:
It's 3:50 a.m. in a hotel in a city you had to look up. Four flights today. You haven't been paid for any of them yet.

One day as a flight attendant, lived from the inside: report at 4:45, a briefing in six minutes, the emergency check nobody sees, boarding (the part that was free for most of the job's history), a bag the size of a dishwasher, a two-hundred-pound cart pushed uphill, a seat belt sign and a coffee pot, twenty-eight minutes to turn a cabin, a fourteen-hour duty day with ten hours of rest, and a kid in row nine who gets your wings.

Based on real research:
• Median pay for flight attendants: $67,130 a year; about 130,800 jobs — U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook, May 2024
• Pay has historically started when the aircraft door closes; Delta added half-rate boarding pay in 2022, American's contract boarding pay began 1 April 2025, United's new contract includes it — NPR, APFA, CBS Chicago
• FAA rule (October 2022): at least 10 consecutive hours of rest for duty periods of 14 hours or less, with no reductions — Federal Register 87 FR 61988
• 146 serious turbulence injuries on US airlines 2009–2021, 116 of them crew — FAA data via AP, December 2022
• One flight attendant per 50 passenger seats — 14 CFR 121.391

srt:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:17,092
Three fifty in the morning. The alarm is in a hotel room, the hotel is in a city you had to check on your phone, and your uniform is hanging on the bathroom door because the iron doesn't work. You have four flights today. You've been paid for none of them yet.

2
00:00:17,492 --> 00:00:35,429
Your name tag says a name. Your face says three fifty. In two hours, two hundred strangers will ask you where to put a bag that is clearly too big, and you will smile at every one of them. The smile is not in your contract. It is, however, expected.

3
00:00:35,829 --> 00:00:49,960
To understand how you ended up in a hotel in a city you can't name, rewind to yesterday afternoon, when your phone rang in the grocery store and a voice said "reserve." You put the groceries back.

4
00:00:50,360 --> 00:01:05,411
Four forty-five. Report time. You badge through a door passengers never see, and you're on duty. Officially. The clock that matters to the airline has started. The clock that pays you has not.

5
00:01:05,811 --> 00:01:24,047
The briefing takes six minutes: four legs, a tight turn in Denver, one wheelchair in row twelve, one nut allergy in row twenty, and a captain who says "we'll try to make up time." You've heard that sentence maybe four thousand times.

6
00:01:24,447 --> 00:01:40,021
You check the emergency equipment. Oxygen, extinguishers, the defibrillator, the slides. Every row. Every flight. You've never used most of it. You check it like you will. That is the whole point.

7
00:01:40,421 --> 00:02:00,648
Five forty. Boarding. Here is the thing nobody outside the airplane knows: for most of the history of this job, this part was free. Your hourly pay started when the door closed. Boarding, the hardest forty minutes of the flight, was a gift to the airline.

8
00:02:01,048 --> 00:02:23,190
That is changing. Delta started paying half rate for boarding in 2022. American started in April 2025. United's new contract includes it too. So this morning you are either paid for the next forty minutes or you are not, depending on your logo. Same bags. Same bins.

9
00:02:23,590 --> 00:02:40,383
The bins. A man with a bag the size of a dishwasher is explaining that it fit last time. You know it did not. You help him anyway, because the alternative is a conversation, and a conversation costs two minutes you don't have.

10
00:02:40,783 --> 00:02:56,058
Row twelve needs the wheelchair. Row twenty needs you to announce the nut allergy. Row thirty-one needs to know if the flight has WiFi. It does. It will not work. You say "it should."

11
00:02:56,458 --> 00:03:12,430
Six ten. The door closes. Somewhere, in a computer in another state, your pay begins. You take a breath. It is the only breath you'll take sitting down until the seat belt sign goes off.

12
00:03:12,830 --> 00:03:32,683
The safety demonstration. You point at the exits. Nobody looks. You hold up the seat belt. Nobody looks. You do it like it matters, because once, on a different plane, it did. You remember that flight. The passengers don't.

13
00:03:33,083 --> 00:03:50,647
The drink cart weighs about two hundred pounds loaded. You push it uphill, because the plane is climbing, down an aisle seventeen inches wide, past elbows, knees, and one bare foot. The foot is always there. The foot is universal.

14
00:03:51,047 --> 00:04:03,735
You do not go to the bathroom. If this sounds familiar, you've met the nurse, the courier, the teacher, the cook and the trucker. Same bladder, thirty-five thousand feet.

15
00:04:04,135 --> 00:04:32,372
The seat belt sign comes on. The captain says "light chop." You are standing with a pot of coffee. Here is what the body pays: between 2009 and 2021 the FAA counted one hundred forty-six serious turbulence injuries on US airlines. One hundred sixteen of them, almost eighty percent, were crew. Not passengers. You. Standing. With the coffee.

16
00:04:32,772 --> 00:04:49,789
You sit on the jump seat, strap in, and watch the cabin bounce. A passenger unbuckles to get his headphones. You say "sir." He sits. You've learned to say "sir" in a tone that stops grown men. It took years.

17
00:04:50,189 --> 00:05:08,749
Landing. Denver. Twenty-eight minutes until the next flight leaves. In that time two hundred people get off, the cabin gets cleaned, and two hundred new people get on. The cleaning is partly you. Nobody mentioned that in the interview either.

18
00:05:09,149 --> 00:05:27,932
You find three newspapers, one diaper, forty-one plastic cups, a phone, a passport, and half a sandwich in a seat pocket. The phone and the passport go back to their people, one of them running. You've stopped asking why. Why doesn't help you clean.

19
00:05:28,332 --> 00:05:53,882
The law lets the airline schedule you for fourteen hours on duty. Then it owes you ten hours of rest. Ten, not nine, since 2022, and the airline can no longer cut it to eight. Those ten hours include the van, the hotel check-in, the shower, and finding food after eleven p.m. Sleep is what's left.

20
00:05:54,282 --> 00:06:15,802
One flight attendant for every fifty seats. That's the rule. On this plane that's four of you for one hundred seventy-six people. If something goes wrong, it's four of you, ninety seconds, and every door. You've practiced it. You hope you never find out.

21
00:06:16,202 --> 00:06:39,240
The median flight attendant in America makes about sixty-seven thousand dollars a year. Not bad. But the hours that count are flight hours, roughly seventy-five to ninety a month. The hours in airports, vans and hotels, in uniform, are what the job is actually made of. You are at work far more than you are paid.

22
00:06:39,640 --> 00:06:49,516
There's also per diem: a couple of dollars an hour for being away from home. It buys the sandwich at the airport. It does not buy the second one.

23
00:06:49,916 --> 00:07:10,914
Leg three. A delay. Weather in Chicago, which is not where you are, but it's where the plane is. You sit at the gate, in uniform, in public, for two hours. The clock that pays you is off. The one that counts your fourteen hours is on.

24
00:07:11,314 --> 00:07:29,027
Leg four. Night. The cabin is dark, the passengers are asleep, and you stand in the back galley eating crackers off a napkin, looking out the small window at a city that is somebody's home. You know the airport code. Not the city.

25
00:07:29,427 --> 00:07:46,768
A kid in row nine is awake and scared. You crouch in the aisle, show her how the window shade works, and give her the pilot wings sticker you keep in your pocket for exactly this. It takes four minutes. It is the best four minutes of your day.

26
00:07:47,168 --> 00:08:00,378
Ten forty p.m. Last door opens. "Buh-bye. Buh-bye. Thank you. Buh-bye." You say it one hundred seventy-six times. You mean it about forty.

27
00:08:00,778 --> 00:08:16,750
The hotel van. Eleven thirty. Check-in. The iron in this room doesn't work either. You hang the uniform on the bathroom door, set the alarm for three fifty, and eat the second sandwich you didn't buy. Lights out.

28
00:08:17,150 --> 00:08:38,596
So why do it. Because when the sign goes off and the sun comes up over a wing at thirty-five thousand feet, you have the best window in the world and nobody in it but you. Because you said "sir" and a man sat down. Because a kid in row nine has your sticker.

29
00:08:38,996 --> 00:08:55,639
And because somewhere, right now, about a hundred and thirty thousand of you are doing exactly this, in a hundred cities, smiling at bags that don't fit, and the whole thing works. Nobody films that either.

30
00:08:56,039 --> 00:09:10,500
That was one day. Tomorrow starts at three fifty, with an iron that doesn't work. Next time: a different job, a different door. Subscribe if you want to be there. And please: the bag does not fit. It never fit.

title: Why It's So Hard to Be a Firefighter
desc:
It's 2:11 a.m. The tones drop. Forty-five seconds later you're on the truck, and your brain still hasn't been consulted.

One shift as a firefighter, lived from the inside: a 24-hour day, the 7 a.m. rig check, seventy pounds of gear, the call nobody expects (most of them are medical), a smoke alarm with a very loud dog, chili that's cold by four, a real fire at 3:40 p.m., what the smoke costs your body, the pay, the volunteers, one ear open at night, and a dumpster with a raccoon watching.

Based on real research:
• Median pay for firefighters: $59,530 a year; about 345,000 jobs — U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook, May 2024
• 36.6 million fire department calls in 2021; about 1.35 million were fires (roughly 1 in 27) and 72% were medical — NFPA, Fire Department Calls
• Occupational exposure as a firefighter classified as Group 1, carcinogenic to humans — IARC Monographs vol. 132, 2022
• About 9% more cancer diagnoses and 14% more cancer deaths than the general US population, cohort of about 30,000 firefighters — NIOSH (Daniels et al.)
• About two in three US firefighters are volunteers — National Volunteer Fire Council / NFPA
• 24/48 and 48/96 shift schedules, about 56 hours a week — IAFF shift-work material
Gear weight and turnout time are rules of thumb; the sleep comparison refers to fatigue studies (Dawson & Reid, 1997).

srt:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:17,787
Two eleven in the morning. The tones drop. You are asleep, then you are standing, then you are in your boots, and your brain has not been consulted about any of it. The light in the bay is already on. It is always already on.

2
00:00:18,187 --> 00:00:29,847
Forty-five seconds from bed to the truck. You have done this about four thousand times. Your body knows where every strap is in the dark. Your body would like to speak to a manager.

3
00:00:30,247 --> 00:00:41,622
To understand why you sleep in your clothes next to a pole, rewind to seven a.m., when you walked into the station with a coffee and a plan, and the plan lasted eleven minutes.

4
00:00:42,022 --> 00:00:59,429
Seven a.m. Shift change. You work twenty-four hours straight, then forty-eight off. Some stations do forty-eight on, ninety-six off. Either way it comes to about fifty-six hours a week, and the week does not care which day it is.

5
00:00:59,829 --> 00:01:15,717
First hour: the rig check. Every hose, every nozzle, every air bottle, every saw. You start the saws. All of them. The neighbours have opinions about this at seven fifteen. You have never once met the neighbours.

6
00:01:16,117 --> 00:01:31,576
Your gear: a tan coat, pants, a hood, gloves, a helmet, and an air pack. All of it together, roughly seventy pounds. You will put it on in under a minute, in the dark, in a truck that is moving.

7
00:01:31,976 --> 00:01:50,998
Here is what nobody outside the station knows: most of your calls are not fires. Not even close. Of the thirty-six million calls US fire departments ran in a year, about one in twenty-seven was a fire. Almost three in four were medical.

8
00:01:51,398 --> 00:02:08,306
So the first call is a man on a kitchen floor with chest pain. You check his pulse, start oxygen, and hold his wife's hand while she looks for his pills. No smoke. No ladder. This is the job. The posters lie a little.

9
00:02:08,706 --> 00:02:23,858
Second call: a car into a pole. Nobody hurt, one airbag, a lot of glass. You sweep the glass. Somebody has to sweep the glass. You've swept more glass than any janitor in the county.

10
00:02:24,258 --> 00:02:38,625
Third call: a smoke alarm with a dead battery at a house with a very loud dog. You change the battery. You pet the dog. The dog does not know you saved its life. The dog is fine with this.

11
00:02:39,025 --> 00:02:53,178
You do not go to the bathroom. If this sounds familiar, you've met the nurse, the courier, the teacher, the cook, the trucker and the flight attendant. Same bladder, louder alarm.

12
00:02:53,578 --> 00:03:07,875
Lunch is at the station, at eleven, because you've learned that one o'clock lunch gets eaten at four. You cook for seven people. The chili is good. The tones drop at the second spoon. The chili is cold at four.

13
00:03:08,275 --> 00:03:22,119
Three forty p.m. A real one. Smoke showing from a second-floor window, a woman on the lawn saying her son is upstairs. Your heart does something. You let it. Then you go in.

14
00:03:22,519 --> 00:03:37,386
Inside, there is no fire like in the movies. There is black. Total black, hot enough to feel through the gloves, and a sound like a highway. You find the stairs with your feet. You find the boy with your hands.

15
00:03:37,786 --> 00:03:55,050
Here is what the body pays. In 2022 the World Health Organization's cancer agency put firefighting in Group 1: carcinogenic to humans. Same group as asbestos. The smoke you just breathed will be with you for years.

16
00:03:55,450 --> 00:04:12,287
A long NIOSH study of thirty thousand firefighters found about nine percent more cancer diagnoses and fourteen percent more cancer deaths than the general public. You know these numbers. You wash your hood anyway. It helps. A little.

17
00:04:12,687 --> 00:04:25,368
The boy is fine. He was in the closet with a cat. You hand him to his mother, and the cat to nobody, because the cat has left. You will not be thanked for the cat. You understand.

18
00:04:25,768 --> 00:04:41,584
Four fifty. You sit on the bumper. Your shirt under the coat is wet through. You drink a bottle of water in one go and the captain says "good job," and that is the whole ceremony. That is all the ceremony you need.

19
00:04:41,984 --> 00:04:56,993
The median firefighter in America makes about fifty-nine thousand five hundred dollars a year. For fifty-six hours a week, that's about twenty dollars an hour. The guy who fixed your furnace charged more. He also got to sleep.

20
00:04:57,393 --> 00:05:14,159
And here's the part the city forgets: most firefighters in America are not paid at all. About two in three are volunteers. They leave dinner, they leave work, they leave a kid's game, and they go in. Then they go back to dinner.

21
00:05:14,559 --> 00:05:29,710
Nine p.m. Dishes. Then the gear: wash the hood, scrub the coat, swap the air bottle, check the saw you already checked. The station is quiet. Quiet makes you nervous. Quiet never lasts.

22
00:05:30,110 --> 00:05:44,477
Ten thirty. You lie down in your clothes. Boots next to the bed, pants folded over them, so you step in and pull up in one move. You do not fall asleep. You lower yourself into a shallow version of it, with one ear open.

23
00:05:44,877 --> 00:05:59,743
Eleven fifty. Tones. A woman who fell in the bathroom. You lift her, check her, make tea, because that is what she needs, and you are back by twelve forty. You lie down again. One ear.

24
00:06:00,143 --> 00:06:13,917
Two eleven. Tones. You already know this one. It's the cold open. Forty-five seconds. Boots, pants, pole, truck. Your body does it. You just come along.

25
00:06:14,317 --> 00:06:31,795
It's a dumpster. A dumpster on fire behind a grocery store, at two in the morning, with nobody around and a raccoon watching from a distance. You put it out in six minutes. The raccoon is unimpressed. So are you.

26
00:06:32,195 --> 00:06:47,346
Four a.m. Back in the bunk. Two hours of sleep in twenty-one hours. Studies say that's about the same as being legally drunk. You will drive a forty-thousand-pound truck at seven. Nobody has a better idea.

27
00:06:47,746 --> 00:07:02,042
Seven a.m. Shift change. You hand over the radio, the rig, and the chili. You drive home with the windows down to get the smoke out of your hair. It doesn't come out. It hasn't come out in nine years.

28
00:07:02,442 --> 00:07:18,045
So why do it. Because a boy is in a closet and you are the one who finds him. Because an old woman gets tea. Because when the tones drop, your body goes, and some small part of you is proud of a body that goes.

29
00:07:18,445 --> 00:07:30,105
And because the station table at eleven, with seven people and a pot of chili and the saws finally quiet, is the best office in the world. For about eleven minutes.

30
00:07:30,505 --> 00:07:45,086
That was one day. Well, one day and one night. Next time: a different job, a different door. Subscribe if you want to be there. And please: change the battery. The dog can't.

title: Why It's So Hard to Be a Construction Worker
desc:
It's 5:15 a.m. It's dark, it's cold, and your knees woke up before you did.

One day as a construction laborer, lived from the inside: the gate at 6:30, the safety meeting that is always about ladders, drywall and concrete carried up stairs because the elevator isn't built yet, a man in a clean white hard hat, the deadliest industry in America, 94 degrees and a concrete pour that won't wait, the pay, the rain days that pay nothing, and a building you can point at six months later.

Based on real research:
• Median pay for construction laborers and helpers: $46,050 a year ($22.14 an hour), below the $49,500 median for all jobs — U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook, May 2024
• 1,075 construction workers died on the job in 2023, the most of any industry and about 1 in 5 of all U.S. work deaths (5,283) — BLS Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries 2023
• Falls, slips and trips caused 421 of those deaths, most from 6 to 30 feet; ladders and stairs were the main source of 109 — BLS CFOI 2023
• Construction was 6% of the workforce but 36% of occupational heat-related deaths, 1992–2016 — CPWR, American Journal of Industrial Medicine
• The industry needed about 439,000 new workers in 2025 — Associated Builders and Contractors
Load weights, start times and rain-day pay describe common practice, not statistics.

srt:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:15,151
Five fifteen in the morning. It is dark, it is cold, and you are already in a pickup with a thermos, two sandwiches and a radio that only gets one station. Your knees woke up before you did. They have complaints.

2
00:00:15,551 --> 00:00:29,776
Somewhere ahead of you is a building that does not exist yet. By the end of the year it will. People will live in it, sleep in it, and never once think about you. That is the deal.

3
00:00:30,176 --> 00:00:43,308
To understand why your knees file complaints, rewind to your first morning on a site: a new hard hat, a borrowed tool belt, and a foreman who looked at your hands and said, "you'll learn."

4
00:00:43,708 --> 00:00:56,390
Six thirty. The gate opens. Work starts at seven, but on a site, seven means you are already dressed, already in the vest, already standing at the safety meeting holding a coffee you will not finish.

5
00:00:56,790 --> 00:01:10,421
The safety meeting takes ten minutes. Today's topic: ladders. Last week's topic: ladders. The topic is always ladders, and there is a reason, and you will hear it in a minute.

6
00:01:10,821 --> 00:01:26,637
Your gear: hard hat, safety glasses, a bright vest, gloves, steel-toe boots, and a tool belt that pulls on your hips before you have put anything useful in it. You will wear all of it for ten hours.

7
00:01:27,037 --> 00:01:46,700
First job: carry. You are a laborer, which means you move what other people install. Drywall, about fifty pounds a sheet. Concrete, eighty pounds a bag. Up two floors. The elevator is not installed yet. You are the elevator.

8
00:01:47,100 --> 00:02:01,823
By nine your shirt is wet, your gloves are grey, and a man in a clean white hard hat walks past with a tablet and says, "looking good." He is the only clean thing on site. You will never find out what is on the tablet.

9
00:02:02,223 --> 00:02:20,082
Here is what nobody outside the fence thinks about. In 2023, one thousand seventy-five construction workers died on the job in America. More than in any other industry. About one in every five people who died at work that year worked in construction.

10
00:02:20,482 --> 00:02:37,889
The biggest killer is not the machines. It is gravity. Falls, slips and trips killed four hundred twenty-one of them. Most of those falls were not from skyscrapers. They were from six to thirty feet. A roof. A scaffold. A ladder.

11
00:02:38,289 --> 00:02:57,524
That is why the topic is always ladders. Ladders and stairs alone killed one hundred nine construction workers in a single year. You check the feet, you check the angle, you tie it off. Every time. Because someone, somewhere, didn't.

12
00:02:57,924 --> 00:03:10,606
You clip your harness to the anchor before you step near the second-floor edge. The harness is hot, it pinches, and you look ridiculous. You wear it anyway. The people who skipped it are part of the number.

13
00:03:11,006 --> 00:03:33,305
You do not go to the bathroom. Well, you do. There is a blue plastic box at the edge of the site, and it has been in the sun since June. If this sounds familiar, you've met the nurse, the courier, the teacher, the cook, the trucker, the flight attendant and the firefighter. Same bladder. Worse bathroom.

14
00:03:33,705 --> 00:03:46,623
Noon. Lunch is a sandwich on an upturned bucket in the only shade on site, which belongs to the dumpster. You eat fast, because thirty minutes is thirty minutes, and the shade moves.

15
00:03:47,023 --> 00:04:03,267
It is ninety-four degrees. The concrete is hotter. The steel is hotter than that. You drink water every fifteen minutes, because the foreman makes you, and because last summer a guy on another crew sat down and didn't get up for a long time.

16
00:04:03,667 --> 00:04:21,953
Here is what the heat costs. Construction is about six percent of America's workers. But over twenty-five years, it accounted for thirty-six percent of all the workers who died from heat. One in three. In a job where summer is the busy season.

17
00:04:22,353 --> 00:04:39,760
Two p.m. The concrete truck arrives early. Concrete does not wait. It starts to set the moment it pours, so the whole crew drops everything, and for ninety minutes nobody talks, nobody sits, and nobody drinks the water they should.

18
00:04:40,160 --> 00:04:53,078
When it is done, the floor is flat, smooth and grey, and it will be under someone's kitchen for fifty years. You scratch the date into the corner with a nail. Nobody told you to. You just do.

19
00:04:53,478 --> 00:05:09,650
The median construction laborer in America makes about forty-six thousand dollars a year. That's about twenty-two dollars an hour. Less than the median for all jobs. For the industry where more people die at work than in any other.

20
00:05:10,050 --> 00:05:26,816
And you are paid by the hour, which means you are paid when you work. When it rains, the site closes. When the site closes, the hour does not exist. Last March it rained for nine days. You remember March.

21
00:05:27,216 --> 00:05:47,117
Meanwhile, the industry says it cannot find people. In 2025 it said it needed four hundred thirty-nine thousand new workers in one year. People who are on time, careful, strong, and happy to stand in ninety-four degrees for twenty-two dollars an hour. It's a long list.

22
00:05:47,517 --> 00:06:00,341
Three thirty. Clean-up. You sweep, stack, coil the cords and lock the tools in the container. The site has to look like nobody was here, so tomorrow everybody can be here again.

23
00:06:00,741 --> 00:06:15,322
Your body hands you the bill on the drive home. Shoulders from the drywall. Knees from the stairs. A back that has carried, by your rough count, a small house. It would like to stop being the elevator.

24
00:06:15,722 --> 00:06:31,253
Four fifteen. You are home. Your daughter asks what you built today. You say, "a floor." She is not impressed. A floor is not a castle. You agree to build a castle on Saturday. Out of blankets.

25
00:06:31,653 --> 00:06:42,814
Dinner. Shower. You are asleep by nine thirty with the light still on, because five fifteen comes whether you are ready or not, and you are never ready.

26
00:06:43,214 --> 00:06:55,397
Six months later, you drive past the building on a Sunday. The windows are in. Somebody has put a plant on a balcony. A kid is waving from the third floor, where you carried drywall in June.

27
00:06:55,797 --> 00:07:06,388
Nobody in that building knows your name. The plant doesn't know. The kid doesn't know. But you know which floor is yours, because you scratched the date into it with a nail.

28
00:07:06,788 --> 00:07:19,042
So why do it. Because at the end of a year, something is standing that wasn't there before, and you can point at it. Most people can't point at anything they did at work. You can point at a building.

29
00:07:19,442 --> 00:07:35,543
And because the crew, the same eight people in the same orange vests eating the same sandwiches in the shade of the same dumpster, is a kind of family nobody else would understand. Loud, rude, and there when the floor needs pouring.

30
00:07:35,943 --> 00:07:53,136
That was one day. Tomorrow starts at five fifteen, in the dark, with a thermos. Next time: a different job, a different door. Subscribe if you want to be there. And next time you pass a site, those people are building your street. Wave.

title: Why It's So Hard to Be the President
desc:
It's 5:45 in the morning. There's a man on the lawn who has been standing there all night. He's not guarding a person. He's guarding the President. That's you.

One day as a fictional President of the United States, lived from the inside: the morning intelligence folder, a schedule cut into fifteen-minute blocks, the aide with the satchel who is never more than a few steps away, a desk where only the hard problems arrive, tens of thousands of letters a day, a car you're not allowed to drive, two hundred handshakes, what the job does to the body, the pay, the grocery bill, forty minutes of dinner, and the phone at 10 p.m.

A fictional, non-political character. No real president is portrayed.

Based on real sources:
• Salary: $400,000 a year plus a $50,000 expense allowance — 3 U.S.C. §102
• The President's Daily Brief has been presented in some form to presidents since 1946 — Office of the Director of National Intelligence
• The military aide's satchel weighs about 45 lb and is never more than a few steps away, elevators included — Atomic Heritage Foundation / National Museum of Nuclear Science & History
• The White House: 132 rooms, 35 bathrooms, 412 doors, 147 windows; the kitchen can serve dinner to 140 guests — whitehouse.gov, "About the White House"
• Tens of thousands of letters, faxes and emails arrive every day — Office of Presidential Correspondence, White House blog (2009, National Archives)
• Elected heads of government lived about 2.7 years less than the runners-up they beat (17 countries, 1722–2015) — Olenski, Abola & Jena, BMJ 2015;351:h6424
• Official records belong to the public — Presidential Records Act of 1978, National Archives
Long-standing practice, not law: presidents don't drive on public roads; the family pays for its own food, billed monthly. The 5:45 wake-up, the 11-minute lunch and the 200 handshakes are the hero's fictional day.

srt:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:16,100
Five forty-five in the morning. You wake before the alarm in a house with one hundred thirty-two rooms and pad to the window. Down on the lawn, in the dark, a man in a dark coat stands very still. He has been there all night.

2
00:00:16,500 --> 00:00:32,960
He is not guarding a person. He is guarding the President of the United States. That's you. You pour coffee into a chipped mug from your hometown diner. It's the only thing here that still uses your first name.

3
00:00:33,360 --> 00:00:48,850
To understand why, rewind to a cold January noon: one hand on a book, one hand raised, an oath of thirty-five words. Then somebody opened a car door for you. You have not opened one yourself since.

4
00:00:49,250 --> 00:01:05,850
Seven a.m. A leather folder waits on your desk: the President's Daily Brief, the intelligence services' summary of what you should know before lunch. Some version of it has been put in front of presidents since 1946.

5
00:01:06,250 --> 00:01:21,560
You read it the way other people read the weather. Except this weather covers the whole planet, and none of it is sunny. Sunny news doesn't need a folder. Your coffee goes cold by page three. It always does.

6
00:01:21,960 --> 00:01:39,820
Eight a.m. Your chief of staff brings the schedule, cut into fifteen-minute blocks. Thirty-one of them. Your name is on every one. Lunch has been shortened twice. He apologises for lunch. He apologises for lunch every day.

7
00:01:40,220 --> 00:01:59,240
And there is one person you are never more than a few steps from: a military aide with a black leather satchel. About forty-five pounds. It goes where you go, elevators included. What's inside is not discussed. Not by you, not by us.

8
00:01:59,640 --> 00:02:16,300
Nine a.m. Meetings. Here is how the desk works: easy problems get solved downstairs. Only the ones nobody else could solve come up to you. So everything on this desk is hard. That's not a bad day. That's the design.

9
00:02:16,700 --> 00:02:33,200
Ten fifteen. A decision. You listen, you ask, you weigh, you choose. Whatever you choose, somebody will be unhappy, and that somebody will have a microphone. You choose anyway. Nobody else is allowed to.

10
00:02:33,600 --> 00:02:49,860
Then you sign things. Lots of things. Under the Presidential Records Act of 1978, your official papers are not yours. They belong to the public. Every memo, every note in the margin. So you doodle very carefully.

11
00:02:50,260 --> 00:03:07,170
Eleven a.m. The mail. Tens of thousands of letters, faxes and emails reach the White House every day, asking you to fix a pothole, a roof, a cat. A whole office reads them. A small stack reaches you. You read every one.

12
00:03:07,570 --> 00:03:30,930
Twelve forty. Lunch: a sandwich at your desk, eleven minutes. If this sounds familiar, you've met the nurse, the courier, the teacher, the cook, the trucker, the flight attendant, the firefighter and the construction worker. Same calendar deciding when you eat. Thirty-five bathrooms. No time for any of them.

13
00:03:31,330 --> 00:03:47,380
Two p.m. An event across town. You get in the back of the car, because presidents do not drive on public roads. The Secret Service drives. The last time you drove, you had to find parking. You miss parking.

14
00:03:47,780 --> 00:04:02,990
The windows don't open. The route was planned days ago by people you've never met. You pass a coffee shop with a line out the door. You would love to stand in that line. You don't do lines anymore.

15
00:04:03,390 --> 00:04:22,910
The agent beside you has an earpiece, a dark suit and one job: to stand between you and danger. She is calm, polite, never more than a door away. She knows how you take your coffee. She has never asked how your day is going. That's professionalism.

16
00:04:23,310 --> 00:04:39,480
At the event you shake two hundred hands, about four seconds each. Every one of those people will remember their four seconds forever. You will remember almost none, and it bothers you every single time.

17
00:04:39,880 --> 00:04:57,710
The quiet part of the job: almost everyone you meet needs something from you. That's not cynical. It's the job description. So when someone asks how you slept, and actually waits for the answer, you notice. It's usually your wife.

18
00:04:58,110 --> 00:05:16,750
Here is what the chair does to the body. A 2015 study in the BMJ compared elected heads of government with the runners-up they beat, in seventeen countries, over almost three hundred years. The winners lived about two point seven years less.

19
00:05:17,150 --> 00:05:34,660
The researchers' careful conclusion: elected leaders may indeed age more quickly. You didn't need a study. You have a mirror. The silver arrived in year one and has been asking for more territory ever since.

20
00:05:35,060 --> 00:05:53,110
The pay, by law: four hundred thousand dollars a year, plus a fifty-thousand-dollar expense allowance. It sounds like a lot. Spread it over a job with no evenings, no weekends and no off switch, and it's a very well-paid night shift.

21
00:05:53,510 --> 00:06:10,880
And the groceries are yours. By long tradition, the President pays for the family's personal food, billed every month, itemised. The kitchen can serve dinner to one hundred forty guests. Your sandwich is on the bill.

22
00:06:11,280 --> 00:06:29,310
Six thirty. Dinner upstairs with your wife. For forty minutes, nobody says "Mr. President." She uses the name on your library card, steals your fries and complains about the crossword. Best forty minutes of the day.

23
00:06:29,710 --> 00:06:44,840
Eight p.m. A thick binder arrives: tomorrow. You read it in an armchair with the chipped mug, now full of tea. Tomorrow has thirty-four blocks. Somebody has already apologised for tomorrow's lunch.

24
00:06:45,240 --> 00:07:03,780
Ten p.m. The phone. Something has happened on the other side of the world, where it's mid-afternoon, and the world does not check your time zone. You listen. You ask three questions. You decide. Then you find your place in the binder.

25
00:07:04,180 --> 00:07:22,570
Eleven thirty. This house has four hundred twelve doors and one hundred forty-seven windows. You have time for exactly one. The man is still on the lawn. Somewhere in the building, the aide with the satchel is awake. A country sleeps because somebody doesn't.

26
00:07:22,970 --> 00:07:40,210
Some days the job feels like a very long meeting in a very beautiful house. Then a letter arrives from a nine-year-old asking if the President has a dog. You answer it yourself, by hand. It goes in the records. Forever.

27
00:07:40,610 --> 00:07:57,510
So why do it. Because almost every decision at that desk lands on somebody you will never meet. A bridge gets fixed. A family gets an answer. A storm gets a response. You never see it land. You sign anyway.

28
00:07:57,910 --> 00:08:15,810
And because the job isn't yours. It was here before you, and it will be here after. You are borrowing the desk, the house, the folder, even the man on the lawn. Every paper belongs to the public. The mug, legally, is yours.

29
00:08:16,210 --> 00:08:32,110
One day the oath will belong to someone else. You'll walk out of a door you didn't open, into a car you're not allowed to drive, and go home. And the first thing you'll do is stand in a line. Any line. On purpose.

30
00:08:32,510 --> 00:08:52,000
That was one day. Tomorrow starts at five forty-five, at the window, with the folder. Next time: a different job, a different door. Subscribe if you want to be there. And if you ever write to the President, keep it short. Lunch is eleven minutes.

title: The Weirdest Jobs in the World (They're All Real)
desc:
Somewhere right now, a person is sniffing an armpit. For money. On purpose. And they're not the strangest worker on this list.

Ten real jobs that sound made up, counted down from ten to one, plus a bonus that's older than all of them: the bicycle fisher of Amsterdam, the professional line stander, the fortune cookie writer, the water slide tester, the golf ball diver, the odor judge, the snake milker, the ice cream taster with a gold spoon, the chick sexer and Tokyo's white-gloved train pushers.

Every worker in this video is a fictional illustration; the jobs and the numbers are real.

Sources:
• 12,000–15,000 bicycles a year recovered from Amsterdam's canals — Guinness World Records; NPR (2022); PRI The World (2015)
• Line standers in Washington: clients have paid about $40–60 an hour — Sunlight Foundation (2011), Washington Express, Roll Call (2009)
• About 4 million fortune cookies a day; a fortune writer of about 30 years stepped back citing writer's block — NPR (17 Feb 2017), NBC News, Money
• Water slide tester: six months, Egypt, Majorca and Turkey, £20,000 a year pro rata, 30-second video applications — First Choice (2013) via Travel Weekly and NPR
• Golf ball divers: murky water worked by feel, 8–10 hours a day, fishing line and alligators, paid per ball — U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Career Outlook (2014)
• Odor judges rate underarm odor, often on a 1–10 scale, after a deodorant-free week — Princeton Consumer Research, Hill Top Research
• Snake milking: about 150 snakes in two hours, 600–1,000 a week, venom for research — Kentucky Reptile Zoo (Freethink, WDRB, WEKU)
• An ice cream taster's taste buds insured for $1 million; gold-plated spoon, spits it out, avoids garlic, onions and spicy food — CBS News, Los Angeles Times
• Chick sexing: vent sexing developed in Japan in the 1920s–30s; about 800–1,400 chicks an hour at around 99% accuracy — Poultry World (2010), Taipei Times (2010)
• Tokyo rush-hour trains averaged 221% of capacity in 1975; the first pushers at Shinjuku were mostly part-time students — Wikipedia "Passenger pusher" (citing LIFE 1964 and The New York Times 1995)
• Professional mourners: ancient Egypt, Victorian "mutes"; a UK service at about £45 for two hours — Funeral Zone, HuffPost UK (2013)
