srt:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:11,750
Somewhere right now, a person is sniffing an armpit. For money. On purpose. With a clipboard. And they are not the strangest worker on this list.

2
00:00:12,150 --> 00:00:24,260
Today: ten real jobs that sound made up. Every one of them exists, somebody is doing it this morning, and somebody's mother is trying to explain it at a family dinner.

3
00:00:24,660 --> 00:00:40,360
Number ten. The bicycle fisher. You work for the water company in Amsterdam. Your boat has a crane with a big steel claw. You lower it into the canal, close it, lift. Bicycle. Again. Bicycle.

4
00:00:40,760 --> 00:00:53,900
Between twelve and fifteen thousand bikes come out of Amsterdam's canals every year. Most were stolen and dumped. Some still have a lock on them, locked to nothing at all. Very secure.

5
00:00:54,300 --> 00:01:07,940
Number nine. The professional line stander. In Washington, people with no time pay people with time to stand in line for them, often outside congressional hearings, sometimes all night.

6
00:01:08,340 --> 00:01:24,720
Clients have paid around forty to sixty dollars an hour. The person actually standing has earned much less. You bring a folding chair, a phone charger and the patience of a statue. At the door, you swap places and go home.

7
00:01:25,120 --> 00:01:38,870
Number eight. The fortune cookie writer. One of America's biggest fortune cookie makers says it bakes around four million cookies a day. Every single one needs a little sentence about your future.

8
00:01:39,270 --> 00:01:56,280
For about thirty years, many of those sentences came from one man, who was also the company's finance chief. Then he stopped. The reason he gave: writer's block. Somewhere, a cookie said: big changes are coming.

9
00:01:56,680 --> 00:02:12,210
Number seven. The water slide tester. In 2013, a British travel company advertised a six-month job: fly to resorts in Egypt, Majorca and Turkey, ride the slides, and report back.

10
00:02:12,610 --> 00:02:27,880
The pay was twenty thousand pounds a year, pro rata. The application was a thirty-second video. The uniform was swim shorts. The hardest part of the job: writing the word splash in a serious tone.

11
00:02:28,280 --> 00:02:43,130
Number six. The golf ball diver. Every pond on a golf course is full of expensive mistakes. You dive in. The water is so murky you work by feel, on your knees in the mud, eight to ten hours a day.

12
00:02:43,530 --> 00:03:00,610
The hazards, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: fishing line that can trap you, objects you can't see, and alligators. You're paid per ball. The balls get cleaned and sold again, ready for their next pond.

13
00:03:01,010 --> 00:03:17,120
Number five. The odor judge. A deodorant company says its product works all day. Somebody has to check. That somebody is you. Volunteers give up their own deodorant for a week. Then they come to the lab.

14
00:03:17,520 --> 00:03:36,430
You lean in, you sniff, and you give the armpit a score, often on a scale from one to ten. Then you come back hours later and do it again. Judges are tested for their sense of smell. It is real science. It is also an armpit.

15
00:03:36,830 --> 00:03:50,590
Number four. The snake milker. At a reptile zoo in Kentucky, venom is collected by hand. You hold the snake's head, it bites a cup covered with a thin film, and the venom runs down the glass.

16
00:03:50,990 --> 00:04:08,890
One milker there has said he does about a hundred and fifty snakes in two hours, about a minute each, six hundred to a thousand a week. The venom goes to research labs and into work on antivenom. The snakes are not grateful.

17
00:04:09,290 --> 00:04:22,820
Number three. The ice cream taster. You taste with a gold-plated spoon, so the metal doesn't change the flavor. You swirl, you think, and you spit it out. Swallowing is for amateurs.

18
00:04:23,220 --> 00:04:36,560
One taster at an American ice cream company had his taste buds insured for one million dollars. He stayed away from garlic, onions and spicy food. Every dinner was a risk assessment.

19
00:04:36,960 --> 00:04:52,140
Number two. The chick sexer. A newborn chick looks the same whether it will grow into a hen or a rooster. A specialist can tell, by looking very closely at a spot almost nobody wants to look at.

20
00:04:52,540 --> 00:05:09,270
The method was developed in Japan in the nineteen twenties and thirties. Training takes years. Top sexers sort around a thousand chicks an hour and aim for ninety-nine percent accuracy. The chicks have no comment.

21
00:05:09,670 --> 00:05:28,140
Number one. The train pusher. In Tokyo's rush hour, the train arrives already full. The doors open. More people get in. And a station attendant in white gloves pushes them, gently and firmly, until the doors can close.

22
00:05:28,540 --> 00:05:50,310
In 1975, Tokyo rush-hour trains ran at an average of two hundred and twenty-one percent of their designed capacity. The first pushers at Shinjuku Station were mostly students working part time. The trains are less crowded now. The white gloves are still there.

23
00:05:50,710 --> 00:06:05,610
A bonus, because it's older than all the others: the professional mourner. In ancient Egypt, people were paid to weep at funerals. Victorian England hired silent mutes in black to stand by the door.

24
00:06:06,010 --> 00:06:21,340
And one British company has offered mourners for hire: around forty-five pounds for two hours, briefed on the life of a person they never met, so they can talk to the family. Somebody has to be good at being sad for strangers.

25
00:06:21,740 --> 00:06:37,300
So why do these jobs exist? Because every strange job solves a real problem. Bikes block canals. Deodorant claims need proof. Trains have to leave on time. Somebody has to do it.

26
00:06:37,700 --> 00:06:54,330
And those somebodies are usually proud of it. Ask a bicycle fisher about the oddest thing in the canal. Ask a chick sexer how fast she is. Ask an odor judge about their day. Actually, maybe don't.

27
00:06:54,730 --> 00:07:07,680
If your job sounds normal, enjoy it. If it doesn't, tell us in the comments. And if you liked this, subscribe. Next time: back to the hardest jobs, one day at a time.

title: Jobs That Will Appear in 10 Years (Some Already Exist)
alts: "10 Jobs of the Future You've Never Heard Of" · "The Jobs of 2036, Explained"
desc:
In ten years, somebody will have a job that sounds like a joke today. Robot teacher. Heat officer. Deepfake detective. Some of these people are already at work.

Ten jobs of the next ten years, counted down from ten to one, plus a bonus twist: the robotaxi helper, the drone fleet supervisor, the deepfake detective, the battery recycler, the chief heat officer, the data center technician, the care robot technician, the wind turbine technician, the AI auditor and the robot trainer. These are forecasts, proposals and targets, not promises, but the first job ads are already out.

Every worker in this video is a fictional illustration; the jobs, rules and numbers come from the sources below.

Sources:
• 170 million jobs created and 92 million displaced by 2030; survey of 1,000+ employers; farmworkers the largest absolute growth (about +35 million) — World Economic Forum, Future of Jobs Report 2025
• Robotaxi remote assistance: helpers give the car advice, not control; about 70 on duty for about 3,000 vehicles — Waymo, "Advice, Not Control" (2026)
• Drones beyond visual line of sight: operations supervisor and flight coordinator roles, aircraft up to 1,320 lb — FAA proposed rule, Part 108 (Aug 2025)
• Deepfake labelling and chatbot disclosure from 2 August 2026 — EU AI Act, Article 50
• High-risk AI in hiring, credit and education, obligations from December 2027 — EU AI Act Annex III, as amended by the Digital Omnibus
• Lithium recovery 50% by end-2027 and 80% by end-2031; recycled content in new batteries from 2031 — EU Batteries Regulation 2023/1542
• First Chief Heat Officer: Miami-Dade County, 2021; later Athens, Freetown and Los Angeles — Miami-Dade County; Arsht-Rockefeller Foundation Resilience Center
• Data centre electricity to more than double by 2030 (about 945 TWh), slightly more than Japan uses today — IEA, Energy and AI (2025)
• Japan needs about 2.72 million care workers in FY2040; about 2.13–2.15 million today — Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare
• Wind turbine service technicians +60%, solar PV installers +48%, 2023–33, the two fastest-growing U.S. occupations — U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics
• Humanoid robot "data collection operator" ad: motion-capture suit, 7+ hours of walking a day, up to 30 lb, up to $48/hour, height 5'7"–5'11" — Business Insider (Aug 2024)

1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:16,270
In ten years, somebody will have a job that sounds like a joke today. Robot teacher. Heat officer. Deepfake detective. Some of these people are already at work, and almost nobody has heard of them.

2
00:00:16,670 --> 00:00:40,200
The World Economic Forum asked more than a thousand employers. Their forecast: about a hundred and seventy million new jobs by 2030, and ninety-two million gone. So here are ten jobs of the next ten years. Forecasts, not promises. But the first job ads are already out.

3
00:00:40,600 --> 00:00:56,630
Number ten. The robotaxi helper. A car with nobody in the driver's seat stops in front of something strange. A fallen tree. A worker waving a flag. It isn't sure what to do. So it asks a human. You.

4
00:00:57,030 --> 00:01:15,190
You sit in an office, maybe in another city. You see what the car sees, and you give it advice. You don't steer. The car still drives itself. One robotaxi company has said it keeps about seventy helpers on duty for around three thousand cars.

5
00:01:15,590 --> 00:01:33,040
Number nine. The drone fleet supervisor. Today, most drones in America must stay where their pilot can see them. The country's aviation regulator has proposed rules to let them fly much farther, beyond anyone's line of sight.

6
00:01:33,440 --> 00:01:54,910
Under that proposal, a drone company needs an operations supervisor and flight coordinators. One person could watch a whole screen of drones, carrying parcels, medicine and cargo, some as heavy as thirteen hundred pounds. You are air traffic control for things with propellers.

7
00:01:55,310 --> 00:02:11,950
Number eight. The deepfake detective. A video shows a famous face saying something terrible. A voice message from your boss asks for an urgent bank transfer. Is it real? Somebody has to check, frame by frame.

8
00:02:12,350 --> 00:02:31,060
Since August 2026, a European Union law says deepfakes must be labeled, and chatbots must tell you they're not human. Labels need checkers. Banks, newsrooms and courts will need people who can look at a face and find the pixel that lies.

9
00:02:31,460 --> 00:02:49,510
Number seven. The battery recycler. Every electric car carries a huge battery under its floor. In the coming years, millions of them will wear out. You open them safely, take them apart, and send the metals back to the factory.

10
00:02:49,910 --> 00:03:12,450
The European Union has set targets: half of the lithium in old batteries must be recovered by the end of 2027, and eighty percent by the end of 2031. From 2031, new batteries must contain some recycled metal. Your old car becomes part of a new one.

11
00:03:12,850 --> 00:03:30,210
Number six. The chief heat officer. In 2021, Miami-Dade County in Florida appointed the world's first. The job: protect a city from heat waves, the way a fire chief protects it from fires.

12
00:03:30,610 --> 00:03:51,060
You plant shade trees, open cooling centers, paint roofs white, and make sure somebody checks on old people living alone when it's over a hundred degrees. Athens, Freetown in Sierra Leone and Los Angeles have hired heat officers too. More cities will follow.

13
00:03:51,460 --> 00:04:08,440
Number five. The data center technician. Every chatbot answer, every video and every photo you upload lives in a giant warehouse full of computers. They run all day, they get hot, and they break. You keep them alive.

14
00:04:08,840 --> 00:04:30,190
The International Energy Agency expects data centers to use more than twice as much electricity in 2030 as in 2024. That's slightly more than the whole of Japan uses today. Somebody has to cool it, power it, and swap the broken parts at three in the morning.

15
00:04:30,590 --> 00:04:48,660
Number four. The care robot technician. Japan is getting older, fast. Its government estimates the country will need about two point seven million care workers in 2040. Today it has fewer than two point two million.

16
00:04:49,060 --> 00:05:09,380
So robots are joining the team: lifting aids, walking helpers, sensors that notice when someone falls at night. They need a person to set them up, fix them and teach the staff. Half engineer, half nurse. The robot does the lifting. You do the caring.

17
00:05:09,780 --> 00:05:26,890
Number three. The wind turbine technician. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, it's the fastest-growing job in America, up about sixty percent in ten years. The office is three hundred feet in the air.

18
00:05:27,290 --> 00:05:45,750
You climb inside the tower, clip on your harness at the top, and fix a machine the size of a bus while the wind tries to steal your hat. Solar panel installers are close behind, up nearly fifty percent. The future runs on people who aren't afraid of heights.

19
00:05:46,150 --> 00:06:04,350
Number two. The AI auditor. Computer programs already help decide who gets a loan, a job interview, or a place at college. What if the program is unfair? It can't explain itself. So somebody checks it before it goes live.

20
00:06:04,750 --> 00:06:28,920
In Europe, AI used for hiring, credit and education counts as high-risk, with strict checks due from December 2027. Auditors test it like detectives: feed it thousands of fake applicants, change one detail, and watch the answer. Same person, different name, different result? Caught.

21
00:06:29,320 --> 00:06:42,810
Number one. The robot trainer. Human-shaped robots are learning to walk, carry boxes and fold laundry. They learn by copying people. And somebody has to be the person they copy.

22
00:06:43,210 --> 00:07:09,030
In 2024, one American carmaker advertised exactly that: wear a motion-capture suit and a headset, walk for more than seven hours a day, carry up to thirty pounds. Pay: up to forty-eight dollars an hour. There was even a height limit, five foot seven to five foot eleven. You are the robot's role model.

23
00:07:09,430 --> 00:07:25,930
And a bonus twist. When the World Economic Forum counted which job will add the most workers by 2030, the winner wasn't a coder or an engineer. It was the farmworker. About thirty-five million more.

24
00:07:26,330 --> 00:07:39,890
Because the world will still need to eat. The farm will just look different: drones over the fields, sensors in the soil, and a farmer checking the tractor's software update before breakfast.

25
00:07:40,290 --> 00:07:58,200
So what do these jobs have in common? Each one exists because a new machine arrived, and somebody had to stand next to it. Cars that drive themselves need a helper. Robots need a teacher. Even the smartest AI needs an auditor.

26
00:07:58,600 --> 00:08:14,840
And here's the good news. Most of these jobs don't need a genius. They need someone calm, careful and curious, with one new skill. The future isn't only hiring robots. It's hiring the people who look after them.

27
00:08:15,240 --> 00:08:27,900
Which one would you take? Robot trainer, heat officer, or deepfake detective? Tell us in the comments. And if you liked this, subscribe. In ten years, we'll check who was right.

title: Why It's So Hard to Be an Underwater Welder
alts: "Why It's So Hard to Be an Underwater Welder (It's Not the 15% Myth)" · "Underwater Welder: The Job Nobody Sees"
desc:
Sixty feet under the Gulf of Mexico, it is so dark you can't see your own glove. It is cold, it is loud, and you are about to start a fire. Underwater.

From dive school and life as a tender, to the first dive, wet welding, Delta P, the bends and 28 days of saturation in a steel tube: what it is really like to be an underwater welder, and why the famous "15% of them die" is a myth (the real number is still frightening).

The diver and everyone in this video are fictional illustrations; the facts and numbers come from the sources below.

Sources:
• Commercial diving school: about 2–7 months; tuition often $15,000–$24,000, plus room, board and gear — Dive Training Magazine; Divers Institute of Technology
• Graduates start as tenders (ADCI Entry Level Tender/Diver)
• Hot-water suits and surface-supplied umbilicals; "make it hot / make it cold" power commands; near-zero visibility, work by touch — AWS Welding Digest (underwater welding safety); Fronius; Kemppi
• Pressure doubles at 33 feet of seawater — basic diving physics
• Wet welds cool fast and can be brittle; critical welds often done dry in a hyperbaric habitat — AWS D3.6M; Fronius
• Commercial diving fatality rate: 158.9 per 100,000 workers per year (2011–2017) — CDC/NIOSH, Maritime Safety and Health (BLS CFOI data)
• Alaska 1990–1997: about 180 per 100,000, 40 times the national average for all workers — CDC MMWR 1998;47(22):452–455
• Delta P (differential pressure) hazards and pre-dive checks — ADCI; HSE
• Saturation: normally no more than 28 days — DMAC 21; decompression from ~650 ft about 8 days — Divers Alert Network (DAN)
• Median annual wage for commercial divers about $61,300 (May 2023) — U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS 49-9092

srt:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:14,600
Sixty feet under the Gulf of Mexico, it is so dark you cannot see your own glove in front of your mask. It is cold, it is loud, and you are about to start a fire. Underwater.

2
00:00:15,000 --> 00:00:32,850
Underwater welders fix what the sea breaks: oil platforms, pipelines, bridges, dams and the hulls of ships. People online call it the most dangerous job in the world. That is not quite true. But it is close enough to matter.

3
00:00:33,250 --> 00:00:47,770
To see why, rewind to dive school. Programs run from about two to seven months, and tuition alone is often fifteen to twenty-four thousand dollars. Room, food and gear come on top.

4
00:00:48,170 --> 00:01:04,700
You learn helmets and hoses, decompression tables, rigging, cutting and welding. Then you learn to do all of it again with your eyes closed, in a tank of murky water, because that is what the real job looks like.

5
00:01:05,100 --> 00:01:14,550
You graduate, and you are not a diver yet. You are a tender. That is the bottom rung of the ladder, and everybody starts there.

6
00:01:14,950 --> 00:01:36,130
A tender carries everything, coils hoses, dresses the diver and watches the bubbles. The diver's hose is called the umbilical. It carries air, a radio line, hot water and sometimes power. If it tangles, someone can die. So you watch it like a hawk.

7
00:01:36,530 --> 00:01:51,190
The work is offshore, on a barge, for weeks at a time. Twelve-hour shifts. A bunk in a room with three strangers. The sea moves all night, and some mornings your stomach moves with it.

8
00:01:51,590 --> 00:02:00,670
Then one morning, after months of tending, the supervisor looks at you and says the words you have been waiting for. You're diving.

9
00:02:01,070 --> 00:02:17,600
Your helmet weighs about thirty pounds on deck. Underwater it floats. Your suit is pumped full of hot water from the surface, because at depth the cold can take a strong person apart in minutes.

10
00:02:18,000 --> 00:02:34,570
You go down a line. At thirty feet the light turns green. At sixty it is almost gone. At thirty-three feet the pressure on your body has already doubled. Every breath you take is packed tighter than the one before.

11
00:02:34,970 --> 00:02:47,340
Down here, visibility is often zero. You work by feel. You find the crack with your fingertips. You learn to read a steel beam the way other people read a book.

12
00:02:47,740 --> 00:03:00,220
Up top, the supervisor watches you through a camera on your helmet and talks to you the whole time. You talk back. When a diver goes quiet, the whole deck goes quiet too.

13
00:03:00,620 --> 00:03:17,070
Now the weld. You hold a rod in a stinger, a welding handle wrapped in insulation. When the arc strikes, it boils the water around it into a pocket of gas and steam. For a moment it is the only light in the ocean.

14
00:03:17,470 --> 00:03:35,540
You never switch the power on yourself. You say, make it hot, and someone on deck closes the switch. When you're done, you say, make it cold. Hundreds of amps run through that rod. You do not let it touch you while it is live.

15
00:03:35,940 --> 00:03:52,640
The cold water also cools the weld too fast, which can make it brittle. So the most important welds are often done dry, inside a pressurized box built around the pipe, called a habitat. You weld in air, sixty feet down.

16
00:03:53,040 --> 00:04:04,420
Here is the number you will see online: fifteen percent of underwater welders die. That is a myth. But the real number is not small.

17
00:04:04,820 --> 00:04:25,140
Federal safety researchers counted about one hundred fifty-nine deaths per hundred thousand commercial divers per year. That is roughly one in six hundred, every year. A study in Alaska found divers were dying at forty times the average rate for all workers.

18
00:04:25,540 --> 00:04:47,730
What kills divers is drowning, tangled hoses, failed gear, and something called Delta P. When water rushes toward an opening, like a pipe intake or a dam gate, it can pin a diver with enormous force. You cannot see it coming. That is why the crew checks for it before every dive.

19
00:04:48,130 --> 00:05:01,600
Then there are the bends. At depth, your body soaks up gas from what you breathe. Come up too fast and it fizzes out as bubbles in your joints, your blood, even your brain.

20
00:05:02,000 --> 00:05:17,180
So you come up slowly, stopping on the line, hanging in the dark and waiting. Sometimes you finish inside a steel chamber on the deck, while the crew eats dinner on the other side of a small round window.

21
00:05:17,580 --> 00:05:30,090
The top rung is saturation diving. When the work is too deep to come up every day, you live under pressure in a steel chamber on the ship for up to twenty-eight days.

22
00:05:30,490 --> 00:05:45,250
You breathe a mix of helium and oxygen. It makes everyone sound like a cartoon. Food comes in through a little airlock. A diving bell carries you down to the job, and back to the chamber to sleep.

23
00:05:45,650 --> 00:06:01,060
Going home takes days. From six hundred fifty feet, decompression can take about eight days, sealed inside the chamber. You cannot leave early. Your body has to let the gas out at its own pace.

24
00:06:01,460 --> 00:06:18,020
And the money? The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics put the median pay for commercial divers at about sixty-one thousand dollars a year. Saturation divers can earn much more, but only for the days they spend under pressure.

25
00:06:18,420 --> 00:06:31,870
You miss birthdays. You call home from a barge with a bad connection. You come back sunburned, tired and a little deaf, and your kid asks why you smell like diesel.

26
00:06:32,270 --> 00:06:45,160
So why does anyone do it? Because bridges have to stand, pipelines cannot leak, and ships cannot sink. Somebody has to go down where nobody can see, and fix it by touch.

27
00:06:45,560 --> 00:07:02,007
Nobody will ever see your best weld. It is sixty feet down, in the dark, holding something together. Would you do this job for sixty thousand a year? Tell us in the comments. And if you liked this, subscribe.

title: The Worst Jobs in History
alts: "10 Worst Jobs in History (Counted Down)" · "History's Worst Jobs Make Yours Look Like a Holiday"
desc:
Before alarm clocks, somebody was paid to wake you up. Before toilets, somebody was paid to empty what was under you.

Ten of the worst jobs in history, counted down from bad to unbelievable: the knocker-upper, the leech collector, the mudlark, the pure finder, the whipping boy, the climbing boy, the gong farmer, the sin eater, the Groom of the Stool and the resurrection man. Plus one bonus job that was actually great.

Everyone in this video is a fictional illustration; the facts and numbers come from the sources below.

Sources:
• Knocker-uppers: long poles and pea shooters, a few pence a week per house; the last are thought to have retired in the 1970s — Wikipedia "Knocker-up"; Historic UK
• Leech collectors: up to ~2,500 leeches a day; France imported 30+ million leeches a year at the height of the craze — Science History Institute, Distillations; Wikipedia
• Mudlarks and pure finders — Henry Mayhew, London Labour and the London Poor (1851); Wikipedia
• Whipping boys: little firm evidence it really happened — Wikipedia; Britannica
• Climbing boys: 1788 minimum age of eight; ended by the Chimney Sweepers Act 1875 (police licensing) — UK Parliament, Living Heritage; Wikipedia
• Gong farmers: night work only; sixpence a day at a royal palace — Wikipedia; Historic UK
• Sin eaters: Welsh and border folklore; how common it was is debated — Wikipedia; Britannica
• Groom of the Stool — Historic Royal Palaces; Wikipedia
• Resurrection men: ~8 guineas a body in 1828; mortsafes; Anatomy Act 1832 — Wikipedia
• Cigar-factory lectores since the 1860s, paid by the workers — Araceli Tinajero, "El Lector" (2010); Wikipedia

00:03:19,249 --> 00:03:20,518
The climbing boy.

61
00:03:20,558 --> 00:03:26,289
Chimneys were narrow, so chimney sweeps
sent small children up inside them,

62
00:03:26,329 --> 00:03:31,753
to scrape the soot off with their hands
and a brush, in total darkness.

63
00:03:32,443 --> 00:03:38,645
A law in seventeen eighty-eight said they
had to be at least eight years old.

64
00:03:38,685 --> 00:03:40,509
It was hardly enforced.

65
00:03:40,549 --> 00:03:43,103
Boys got stuck, burned and sick.

66
00:03:43,143 --> 00:03:48,533
It took until eighteen seventy-five for
Britain to finally stop it,

67
00:03:48,573 --> 00:03:52,019
by making every sweep get a police
licence.

68
00:03:52,709 --> 00:03:53,609
Number four.

69
00:03:53,649 --> 00:03:54,864
The gong farmer.

70
00:03:54,904 --> 00:03:59,724
In Tudor England, toilets emptied into
deep pits called gongs.

71
00:03:59,764 --> 00:04:05,603
When a pit was full, a gong farmer climbed
in and shoveled it out, by hand,

72
00:04:05,643 --> 00:04:06,622
into barrels.

73
00:04:07,312 --> 00:04:12,879
Because the job was so disgusting, they
were only allowed to work at night.

74
00:04:12,919 --> 00:04:18,262
One record says gong farmers at a royal
palace were paid sixpence a day,

75
00:04:18,302 --> 00:04:20,505
which was actually good money.

76
00:04:20,545 --> 00:04:23,570
Nobody wanted to know how they earned it.

77
00:04:24,260 --> 00:04:25,213
Number three.

78
00:04:25,253 --> 00:04:26,283
The sin eater.

79
00:04:26,323 --> 00:04:32,090
In parts of Wales and western England,
folklore says that when someone died,

80
00:04:32,130 --> 00:04:35,070
bread and salt were placed on the body.

81
00:04:35,110 --> 00:04:40,572
A poor stranger was paid to eat it, and
with it, the dead person's sins.

82
00:04:41,262 --> 00:04:44,117
Afterwards, the sin eater was shunned,

83
00:04:44,157 --> 00:04:47,470
because he now carried everyone else's
sins.

84
00:04:47,510 --> 00:04:51,737
Historians still argue about how common
this really was.

85
00:04:51,777 --> 00:04:54,785
But it was written down, more than once.

86
00:04:54,825 --> 00:04:57,986
Imagine putting that on a job application.

87
00:04:58,676 --> 00:04:59,506
Number two.

88
00:04:59,546 --> 00:05:01,325
The Groom of the Stool.

89
00:05:01,365 --> 00:05:03,303
This one was a royal job.

90
00:05:03,343 --> 00:05:06,943
The groom helped the Tudor king on the
toilet.

91
00:05:06,983 --> 00:05:07,734
Every day.

92
00:05:07,774 --> 00:05:08,604
Personally.

93
00:05:09,294 --> 00:05:10,854
And here's the twist.

94
00:05:10,894 --> 00:05:14,360
It was one of the most powerful jobs at
court.

95
00:05:14,400 --> 00:05:17,561
The groom was the man closest to the king,

96
00:05:17,601 --> 00:05:21,219
and became something like his private
secretary.

97
00:05:21,259 --> 00:05:25,562
The worst job on paper was the one every
nobleman wanted.

98
00:05:26,252 --> 00:05:27,102
Number one.

99
00:05:27,142 --> 00:05:28,800
The resurrection man.

100
00:05:28,840 --> 00:05:31,954
In the seventeen and eighteen hundreds,

101
00:05:31,994 --> 00:05:38,181
medical schools needed bodies to study,
and there were not enough legal ones.

102
00:05:38,221 --> 00:05:44,003
So, at night, men dug up fresh graves and
sold the bodies to anatomists.

103
00:05:44,693 --> 00:05:50,153
In eighteen twenty-eight, a body could
sell for around eight guineas,

104
00:05:50,193 --> 00:05:53,102
more than a laborer earned in months.

105
00:05:53,142 --> 00:05:56,291
Families guarded graves with iron cages.

106
00:05:56,331 --> 00:06:01,870
The trade only faded after the Anatomy Act
of eighteen thirty-two gave

107
00:06:01,910 --> 00:06:04,262
doctors legal bodies to study.

108
00:06:04,952 --> 00:06:09,007
And a bonus, because history wasn't all
terrible.

109
00:06:09,047 --> 00:06:13,352
In Cuban cigar factories, from the
eighteen sixties,

110
00:06:13,392 --> 00:06:19,286
the workers paid a man to sit on a
platform and read to them while they

111
00:06:19,326 --> 00:06:23,632
rolled cigars: newspapers, novels, even
Shakespeare.

112
00:06:24,322 --> 00:06:26,185
He was called the lector.

113
00:06:26,225 --> 00:06:31,135
The workers chose the books, and paid him
out of their own wages.

114
00:06:31,175 --> 00:06:35,779
Some cigars are even named after the
novels the lectors read.

115
00:06:35,819 --> 00:06:38,521
In Cuba, the job still exists today.

116
00:06:39,211 --> 00:06:42,039
So what do these jobs have in common?

117
00:06:42,079 --> 00:06:46,534
Each one existed because somebody needed a
problem solved,

118
00:06:46,574 --> 00:06:49,480
and there was no machine to do it yet.

119
00:06:49,520 --> 00:06:50,643
No alarm clock.

120
00:06:50,683 --> 00:06:51,418
No sewers.

121
00:06:51,458 --> 00:06:52,348
No medicine.

122
00:06:52,388 --> 00:06:54,828
Just a person, willing to do it.

123
00:06:55,518 --> 00:07:00,267
And for most of them, that person was
poor, young, or both.

124
00:07:00,307 --> 00:07:03,758
The next time your job feels bad,
remember:

125
00:07:03,798 --> 00:07:09,602
at least nobody asked you to wade into a
marsh and wait for the leeches.

126
00:07:10,292 --> 00:07:13,645
Which of these would you take, if you had
to?

127
00:07:13,685 --> 00:07:15,455
Tell us in the comments.

128
00:07:15,495 --> 00:07:17,943
And if you liked this, subscribe.

129
00:07:17,983 --> 00:07:18,697
Next time,

130
00:07:18,737 --> 00:07:24,050
we'll look at the jobs from our own
century that history will laugh at.

title: 10 Jobs AI Can't Replace
alts: "Jobs AI Still Can't Do (Even in 2026)" · "Who AI Can't Replace: 10 Jobs Based on Real Data"
desc:
AI can write essays, draw pictures and translate languages in seconds. So, is your job next?

We flipped the question: ten jobs AI can barely touch, counted down, based on real research. Roofers, plumbers, electricians, wind turbine technicians, phlebotomists, nurse practitioners, home health aides and more. And why the "safe" jobs are safe: hands, unpredictable places, and people who trust you.

Everyone in this video is a fictional illustration; the facts and numbers come from the sources below.

Sources:
• Microsoft Research, "Working with AI: Measuring the Occupational Implications of Generative AI" (Tomlinson et al., 2025, arXiv 2507.07935): ~200,000 Copilot conversations; least applicable jobs include phlebotomists, nursing assistants, hazardous materials removal workers, embalmers, roofers and massage therapists; most applicable include interpreters and translators, historians, writers and customer service
• U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Employment Projections 2024–34: wind turbine service technicians +49.9%; nurse practitioners +40.1%; electricians +9% (~77,400 jobs); home health and personal care aides +739,800 jobs (most of any occupation)
• World Economic Forum, Future of Jobs Report 2025: ~170 million jobs created and ~92 million displaced by 2030; fastest declining: postal clerks, bank tellers, data entry clerks
• Moravec's paradox — Hans Moravec, Mind Children (1988)

1
00:00:00,250 --> 00:00:06,419
AI can now write essays, draw pictures and
translate languages in seconds.

2
00:00:06,459 --> 00:00:11,454
So millions of people are asking a very
reasonable question: is my job next?

3
00:00:12,104 --> 00:00:13,594
Let's flip it.

4
00:00:13,634 --> 00:00:17,546
Here are ten jobs AI can barely touch,
counted down, based on real research.

5
00:00:17,586 --> 00:00:21,299
Some of them pay better than you'd think.

6
00:00:21,339 --> 00:00:25,074
And one of them, you've probably never
thought about.

7
00:00:25,724 --> 00:00:27,260
Number ten.

8
00:00:27,300 --> 00:00:27,408
The roofer.

9
00:00:27,448 --> 00:00:28,316
In twenty twenty-five,

10
00:00:28,356 --> 00:00:35,084
Microsoft researchers looked at two
hundred thousand real conversations with

11
00:00:35,124 --> 00:00:41,100
their AI assistant, and measured which
jobs it could actually help with.

12
00:00:41,140 --> 00:00:43,583
Roofers landed near the very bottom.

13
00:00:44,233 --> 00:00:45,450
It makes sense.

14
00:00:45,490 --> 00:00:47,090
Every roof is different.

15
00:00:47,130 --> 00:00:52,006
It's steep, it's wet, it's windy, and the
work is done by hand,

16
00:00:52,046 --> 00:00:53,860
thirty feet up.

17
00:00:53,900 --> 00:00:57,058
A chatbot can explain how shingles work.

18
00:00:57,098 --> 00:00:58,601
It cannot climb a ladder.

19
00:00:59,251 --> 00:01:00,251
Number nine.

20
00:01:00,291 --> 00:01:01,885
The massage therapist.

21
00:01:01,925 --> 00:01:03,212
Same study, same result.

22
00:01:03,252 --> 00:01:09,526
The whole job is hands, pressure, and
feeling what the body is doing,

23
00:01:09,566 --> 00:01:10,975
muscle by muscle.

24
00:01:11,625 --> 00:01:16,574
AI can guess where your back hurts, if you
describe it well.

25
00:01:16,614 --> 00:01:17,444
But it can't feel the knot.

26
00:01:17,484 --> 00:01:23,261
And most people would rather not be
massaged by a robot arm anyway.

27
00:01:23,911 --> 00:01:25,244
Number eight.

28
00:01:25,284 --> 00:01:26,177
The plumber.

29
00:01:26,217 --> 00:01:30,362
Every house is a puzzle: old pipes, odd
angles,

30
00:01:30,402 --> 00:01:32,684
a leak somewhere behind a wall.

31
00:01:32,724 --> 00:01:36,398
You work on your back, under a sink,
mostly by feel.

32
00:01:37,048 --> 00:01:38,846
Robots are great in a factory,

33
00:01:38,886 --> 00:01:43,457
where every part is in the same place
every time.

34
00:01:43,497 --> 00:01:48,926
A crawl space under a hundred-year-old
house is the exact opposite.

35
00:01:48,966 --> 00:01:52,149
That's why plumbers keep getting calls.

36
00:01:52,799 --> 00:01:54,345
Number seven.

37
00:01:54,385 --> 00:01:55,088
The electrician.

38
00:01:55,128 --> 00:01:56,348
In the United States,

39
00:01:56,388 --> 00:02:02,077
jobs for electricians are projected to
grow nine percent by twenty

40
00:02:02,117 --> 00:02:03,872
thirty-four.

41
00:02:03,912 --> 00:02:06,695
That's about seventy-seven thousand new
jobs.

42
00:02:07,345 --> 00:02:11,703
And here's the irony: the AI boom needs
them.

43
00:02:11,743 --> 00:02:13,325
Every new data center,

44
00:02:13,365 --> 00:02:19,630
every charging station and every solar
roof has to be wired by a human with a

45
00:02:19,670 --> 00:02:21,218
licence and steady hands.

46
00:02:21,868 --> 00:02:23,084
Number six.

47
00:02:23,124 --> 00:02:24,746
The wind turbine technician.

48
00:02:24,786 --> 00:02:28,892
It's one of the fastest growing jobs in
America,

49
00:02:28,932 --> 00:02:34,138
with employment projected to grow almost
fifty percent by twenty thirty-four.

50
00:02:34,788 --> 00:02:40,289
The office is a box at the top of a tower,
hundreds of feet up, in the wind.

51
00:02:40,329 --> 00:02:45,514
You climb, you clip in, and you fix a
machine the size of a bus.

52
00:02:45,554 --> 00:02:47,984
No software update does that for you.

53
00:02:48,634 --> 00:02:49,558
Number five.

54
00:02:49,598 --> 00:02:52,281
The hazardous materials removal worker.

55
00:02:52,321 --> 00:02:54,199
Asbestos, lead, toxic waste.

56
00:02:54,239 --> 00:02:59,604
Somebody has to suit up, go in, and
carefully take it out.

57
00:03:00,254 --> 00:03:05,980
In the Microsoft study, this job ranked
among the ten least touched by AI.

58
00:03:06,020 --> 00:03:10,831
Every building is different, every mistake
is dangerous,

59
00:03:10,871 --> 00:03:13,344
and the rules are strict for a reason.

60
00:03:13,994 --> 00:03:15,413
Number four.

61
00:03:15,453 --> 00:03:16,188
The phlebotomist.

62
00:03:16,228 --> 00:03:19,624
That's the person who draws your blood.

63
00:03:19,664 --> 00:03:24,701
In the Microsoft study, it came out as the
job AI touches least of all.

64
00:03:25,351 --> 00:03:27,857
Finding a vein is a skill.

65
00:03:27,897 --> 00:03:33,032
Calming a nervous patient, or a crying
five-year-old, is another one.

66
00:03:33,072 --> 00:03:36,750
Doing both in under a minute is something
no machine does yet.

67
00:03:37,400 --> 00:03:38,992
Number three.

68
00:03:39,032 --> 00:03:39,420
The embalmer.

69
00:03:39,460 --> 00:03:44,009
It's a quiet job most people never think
about.

70
00:03:44,049 --> 00:03:47,617
Embalmers prepare the dead, so families
can say goodbye.

71
00:03:48,267 --> 00:03:52,143
It takes skill, steady hands and a lot of
respect.

72
00:03:52,183 --> 00:03:57,636
It also made Microsoft's list of the jobs
least affected by AI.

73
00:03:57,676 --> 00:04:00,415
Some work is simply too human to hand
over.

74
00:04:01,065 --> 00:04:02,034
Number two.

75
00:04:02,074 --> 00:04:04,005
The nurse practitioner.

76
00:04:04,045 --> 00:04:09,413
These are advanced nurses who can examine,
diagnose and treat patients.

77
00:04:09,453 --> 00:04:15,184
It's the fastest growing healthcare job in
the United States,

78
00:04:15,224 --> 00:04:19,120
projected to grow about forty percent by
twenty thirty-four.

79
00:04:19,770 --> 00:04:25,034
AI will help them, by writing notes,
checking scans and flagging risks.

80
00:04:25,074 --> 00:04:30,358
But someone still has to sit with the
patient, notice what's wrong,

81
00:04:30,398 --> 00:04:33,646
and be trusted with the decision.

82
00:04:34,296 --> 00:04:35,494
Number one.

83
00:04:35,534 --> 00:04:36,903
The home health aide.

84
00:04:36,943 --> 00:04:43,193
These workers help elderly and sick people
at home: getting up, washing,

85
00:04:43,233 --> 00:04:45,491
eating, taking medicine.

86
00:04:45,531 --> 00:04:47,531
They are the human side of care.

87
00:04:48,181 --> 00:04:49,768
In the United States,

88
00:04:49,808 --> 00:04:55,377
this job is projected to add about seven
hundred and forty thousand jobs by

89
00:04:55,417 --> 00:04:57,770
twenty thirty-four.

90
00:04:57,810 --> 00:05:00,481
That's more than any other occupation.

91
00:05:00,521 --> 00:05:05,888
And nursing assistants ranked second in
Microsoft's list of jobs least

92
00:05:05,928 --> 00:05:07,122
affected by AI.

93
00:05:07,772 --> 00:05:11,278
So, which jobs are the most exposed?

94
00:05:11,318 --> 00:05:16,024
In the same study: interpreters and
translators, historians, writers,

95
00:05:16,064 --> 00:05:18,856
and customer service.

96
00:05:18,896 --> 00:05:22,218
And the World Economic Forum expects bank
tellers,

97
00:05:22,258 --> 00:05:26,529
data entry clerks and postal clerks to
shrink the most.

98
00:05:27,179 --> 00:05:31,191
That doesn't mean those people simply
disappear.

99
00:05:31,231 --> 00:05:33,162
It means the tasks change.

100
00:05:33,202 --> 00:05:39,186
The World Economic Forum still expects
about a hundred and seventy million

101
00:05:39,226 --> 00:05:44,842
new jobs worldwide by twenty thirty,
against ninety-two million lost.

102
00:05:45,492 --> 00:05:48,667
So why are the safe jobs safe?

103
00:05:48,707 --> 00:05:49,953
In the nineteen eighties,

104
00:05:49,993 --> 00:05:55,388
a robotics researcher named Hans Moravec
noticed something strange.

105
00:05:55,428 --> 00:06:00,328
For computers, the hard things, like chess
and math, are easy.

106
00:06:00,368 --> 00:06:05,776
The easy things, like walking, grabbing
and seeing, are incredibly hard.

107
00:06:06,426 --> 00:06:07,734
That is still mostly true.

108
00:06:07,774 --> 00:06:09,338
The jobs that AI

109
00:06:09,378 --> 00:06:15,762
can't replace need hands, unpredictable
places, and people who trust you.

110
00:06:15,802 --> 00:06:20,599
If your work has all three, a robot is not
coming for it anytime soon.

111
00:06:21,249 --> 00:06:24,089
Which job on this list would you pick?

112
00:06:24,129 --> 00:06:26,097
Tell us in the comments.

113
00:06:26,137 --> 00:06:28,740
And if you liked this, subscribe.

114
00:06:28,780 --> 00:06:33,365
Next time, we'll look at the jobs AI is
already changing, right now.

title: The Loneliest Jobs on Earth
alts: "10 Loneliest Jobs on Earth (Counted Down)" · "Jobs Where You Don't See Anyone for Months"
desc:
Imagine going to work and not seeing another human face for weeks. For some people, that's the job description.

Ten of the loneliest jobs on Earth, counted down: the lighthouse keeper, the penguin postmaster of Port Lockroy, the fire lookout, the sheepherder, the long-haul trucker, the island weather observer, the saturation diver, the submariner, the South Pole winter crew, and the Concordia crew that space agencies study to prepare for Mars. Plus a bonus from history: the Apollo command module pilot who circled the Moon alone.

Everyone in this video is a fictional illustration; the facts and numbers come from the sources below.

Sources:
• Lighthouse keepers: Trinity House "A fine farewell" (North Foreland, keepers withdrawn November 1998); NPR (Dec 2023) and National Park Service, Boston Light (last official U.S. keeper retired end of 2023)
• Port Lockroy: UK Antarctic Heritage Trust recruitment coverage (Fox Weather 2024): small team, about five months a season, gentoo penguin counts, no running water, tens of thousands of postcards
• Fire lookouts: HistoryLink.org essay 8034 (Jack Kerouac, 63 days on Desolation Peak, 1956); National Forest Foundation "A Room With a View"
• Sheepherders: High Country News; The Journal (Cortez); NPR "Sheepherding remains a lonely life"; Western Horseman on Basque herders ("struck by sagebrush")
• Truck drivers: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook (about 2.2 million heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers, 2024)
• Gough Island: ACAP and SANAP (overwintering teams of about 13 months; annual relief voyage of the S.A. Agulhas II)
• Saturation diving: DMAC guidance note 21 (28-day limit); Atlas Obscura, gCaptain (heliox, multi-day decompression)
• Submarines: U.S. Navy fact file, Ballistic Missile Submarines (average patrol about 77 days); The War Horse (familygrams of about 40 words)
• South Pole: NOAA GML (winter crew isolated mid-February to late October); The Antarctic Sun (crews of about 40–48)
• Concordia: European Space Agency (no plane in winter, nearest people 600 km away at Vostok, about four months without sun, down to −80 °C, "White Mars")
• Apollo 11: Michael Collins, Carrying the Fire (1974); NASA commentary "Not since Adam has any human known such solitude"; about 47 minutes without radio contact per orbit

Boston Light,

20
00:00:59,876 --> 00:01:03,700
retired at the end of twenty twenty-three.

21
00:01:04,350 --> 00:01:05,792
Number nine.

22
00:01:05,832 --> 00:01:06,994
The penguin postmaster.

23
00:01:07,034 --> 00:01:11,986
On a tiny island in Antarctica, there's a
post office called Port Lockroy.

24
00:01:12,026 --> 00:01:17,540
Every season, a handful of people run it
for about five months.

25
00:01:18,190 --> 00:01:21,921
They sell stamps to cruise ship
passengers,

26
00:01:21,962 --> 00:01:24,345
send tens of thousands of postcards,

27
00:01:24,385 --> 00:01:28,453
and count the gentoo penguins nesting
right outside.

28
00:01:28,493 --> 00:01:30,989
There's no running water.

29
00:01:31,029 --> 00:01:35,570
And when the ship leaves, it's just you,
and a lot of penguins.

30
00:01:36,220 --> 00:01:37,616
Number eight.

31
00:01:37,656 --> 00:01:38,566
The fire lookout.

32
00:01:38,606 --> 00:01:44,169
You live in a tiny glass cabin on top of a
mountain, all summer,

33
00:01:44,209 --> 00:01:46,716
watching the forest for smoke.

34
00:01:46,756 --> 00:01:47,794
In nineteen fifty-six,

35
00:01:47,834 --> 00:01:54,158
the writer Jack Kerouac did this job for
sixty-three days on Desolation Peak,

36
00:01:54,198 --> 00:01:55,550
in Washington State.

37
00:01:56,200 --> 00:01:56,802
The U.S.

38
00:01:56,842 --> 00:02:01,316
Forest Service once had thousands of
staffed lookouts.

39
00:02:01,356 --> 00:02:06,889
Today, planes, cameras and satellites do
most of the watching.

40
00:02:06,929 --> 00:02:11,050
But a few hundred towers are still staffed
every fire season.

41
00:02:11,700 --> 00:02:13,258
Number seven.

42
00:02:13,298 --> 00:02:14,933
The sheepherder.

43
00:02:14,973 --> 00:02:16,443
In the American West,

44
00:02:16,483 --> 00:02:21,746
herders follow huge flocks across
mountains and desert for months.

45
00:02:21,786 --> 00:02:24,381
Home is a small sheep wagon.

46
00:02:24,421 --> 00:02:27,270
The company is a horse and a couple of
dogs.

47
00:02:27,920 --> 00:02:33,370
Today, most of these herders come from
Peru, on temporary work visas.

48
00:02:33,410 --> 00:02:37,741
Many say the hardest part isn't the cold
or the coyotes.

49
00:02:37,781 --> 00:02:40,223
It's having nobody to talk to.

50
00:02:40,263 --> 00:02:44,755
Old Basque herders even had a name for
going a bit strange out there:

51
00:02:44,795 --> 00:02:46,340
struck by sagebrush.

52
00:02:46,990 --> 00:02:47,782
Number six.

53
00:02:47,822 --> 00:02:48,952
The long-haul truck driver.

54
00:02:48,992 --> 00:02:54,655
This one might surprise you, because it's
a huge job.

55
00:02:54,695 --> 00:02:58,410
America has about two point two million
heavy truck drivers.

56
00:02:59,060 --> 00:03:04,152
But many long-haul drivers spend long
stretches on the road, far from home.

57
00:03:04,192 --> 00:03:10,832
They eat alone, sleep in the cab, and work
nights, weekends and holidays.

58
00:03:10,872 --> 00:03:15,740
Surrounded by millions of people, and they
know none of them.

59
00:03:16,390 --> 00:03:18,018
Number five.

60
00:03:18,058 --> 00:03:19,304
The island weather observer.

61
00:03:19,344 --> 00:03:23,293
Gough Island sits in the middle of the
South Atlantic,

62
00:03:23,333 --> 00:03:28,522
more than two thousand kilometres from the
nearest continent.

63
00:03:28,561 --> 00:03:30,940
South Africa runs a weather station there.

64
00:03:31,590 --> 00:03:36,545
A small team lives on the island for about
thirteen months.

65
00:03:36,585 --> 00:03:41,405
One ship comes once a year, with new
people and fresh food.

66
00:03:41,445 --> 00:03:44,390
If you forgot something, you wait until
next year.

67
00:03:45,040 --> 00:03:46,439
Number four.

68
00:03:46,479 --> 00:03:47,632
The saturation diver.

69
00:03:47,672 --> 00:03:51,189
These divers repair pipelines deep under
the sea.

70
00:03:51,229 --> 00:03:54,650
Instead of going up and down every day,

71
00:03:54,690 --> 00:03:59,311
they live under pressure in a sealed steel
chamber,

72
00:03:59,351 --> 00:04:00,990
for up to twenty-eight days.

73
00:04:01,640 --> 00:04:04,811
They breathe a mix of helium and oxygen,

74
00:04:04,851 --> 00:04:07,942
which makes their voices sound squeaky.

75
00:04:07,982 --> 00:04:12,117
And when the job ends, they can't just
step outside.

76
00:04:12,157 --> 00:04:16,372
Coming back to normal pressure can take
several days,

77
00:04:16,412 --> 00:04:18,580
sometimes more than a week.

78
00:04:19,230 --> 00:04:19,895
Number three.

79
00:04:19,935 --> 00:04:21,455
The submariner.

80
00:04:21,495 --> 00:04:26,101
On an American ballistic missile
submarine,

81
00:04:26,141 --> 00:04:31,616
a patrol usually lasts two to three
months, almost all of it underwater.

82
00:04:31,656 --> 00:04:32,793
No sunlight.

83
00:04:32,833 --> 00:04:33,690
No internet.

84
00:04:34,340 --> 00:04:37,107
The whole point is to stay hidden.

85
00:04:37,147 --> 00:04:41,814
Families can send short messages, about
forty words each.

86
00:04:41,854 --> 00:04:46,560
For months, that might be all the news you
get from home.

87
00:04:47,210 --> 00:04:48,566
Number two.

88
00:04:48,606 --> 00:04:51,123
The South Pole winter crew.

89
00:04:51,163 --> 00:04:57,039
Every February, the last plane leaves the
Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station.

90
00:04:57,079 --> 00:04:59,350
Around forty people stay behind.

91
00:05:00,000 --> 00:05:04,096
No flights in or out until about October.

92
00:05:04,136 --> 00:05:05,111
Six months of darkness.

93
00:05:05,151 --> 00:05:11,148
Temperatures that can drop below minus one
hundred degrees Fahrenheit.

94
00:05:11,188 --> 00:05:15,050
If something goes wrong, help is very,
very far away.

95
00:05:15,700 --> 00:05:17,218
Number one.

96
00:05:17,258 --> 00:05:18,779
The winter crew at Concordia.

97
00:05:18,819 --> 00:05:23,536
It's a French and Italian station, high on
the Antarctic ice.

98
00:05:23,576 --> 00:05:27,776
In winter, about a dozen people live
there.

99
00:05:27,816 --> 00:05:29,325
No plane can reach them,

100
00:05:29,365 --> 00:05:33,090
and the nearest humans are six hundred
kilometres away.

101
00:05:33,740 --> 00:05:37,289
The sun disappears for about four months,

102
00:05:37,329 --> 00:05:41,318
and it can get down to minus eighty
degrees Celsius.

103
00:05:41,358 --> 00:05:46,494
The European Space Agency sends a doctor
every year to study the crew.

104
00:05:46,534 --> 00:05:51,410
They call it White Mars, because it's
practice for the first trip to Mars.

105
00:05:52,060 --> 00:05:54,743
And a bonus, from history.

106
00:05:54,784 --> 00:05:56,707
The Apollo command module pilot.

107
00:05:56,747 --> 00:06:02,299
In nineteen sixty-nine, while two
astronauts walked on the Moon,

108
00:06:02,339 --> 00:06:05,150
Michael Collins circled above it, alone.

109
00:06:05,800 --> 00:06:08,618
Every time he passed behind the Moon,

110
00:06:08,658 --> 00:06:13,745
he lost radio contact with Earth for about
forty-seven minutes.

111
00:06:13,785 --> 00:06:19,816
A NASA commentator said: not since Adam
has any human known such solitude.

112
00:06:19,856 --> 00:06:22,789
But Collins wrote that he didn't feel
lonely.

113
00:06:22,829 --> 00:06:26,640
He felt awareness, confidence, almost joy.

114
00:06:27,290 --> 00:06:29,857
So why would anyone choose this?

115
00:06:29,897 --> 00:06:34,908
People who do these jobs often talk about
the same things.

116
00:06:34,948 --> 00:06:35,070
Quiet.

117
00:06:35,110 --> 00:06:36,146
Focus.

118
00:06:36,186 --> 00:06:40,160
And a view that almost nobody else on
Earth gets to see.

119
00:06:40,810 --> 00:06:44,232
Space agencies study these crews closely,

120
00:06:44,272 --> 00:06:49,519
because the first people going to Mars
will face the same thing.

121
00:06:49,559 --> 00:06:53,202
And maybe there's a lesson for the rest of
us too.

122
00:06:53,243 --> 00:06:56,419
Loneliness isn't only about distance.

123
00:06:56,459 --> 00:06:58,790
It's about having nobody to talk to.

124
00:06:59,440 --> 00:07:02,034
Which of these jobs could you handle?

125
00:07:02,074 --> 00:07:03,856
Tell us in the comments.

126
00:07:03,896 --> 00:07:06,263
And if you liked this, subscribe.

127
00:07:06,303 --> 00:07:11,130
Next time: jobs that pay insanely well,
but nobody wants them.
